questions.text: Which of the following diagnoses must be excluded first in a teenage boy presenting with acute left-sided testicular pain?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion is a true surgical emergency — testicular salvage falls sharply after 6 hours, so it must always be excluded first in any acute scrotum presentation.

questions.text: Regarding varicocele in young males, which of the following is true?
options: More common on the left side
More common on the right side
originalOptions: More common on the left side
More common on the right side
questions.correctAnswer: A) More common on the left side
questions.correctAnswerText: More common on the left side
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle and is compressed by the "nutcracker effect" (aorta and SMA), causing higher venous pressure and predisposing to left-sided varicocele.

questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with dysuria, cloudy urine, and a tender, swollen right testis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An older man with dysuria (UTI symptoms) and a tender, swollen testis fits epididymitis, typically caused by E. coli and other Gram-negative bacilli in this age group.

questions.text: What is the sonographic hallmark of testicular torsion?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Absence of intratesticular blood flow
questions.explanation: Decreased or absent blood flow on scrotal Doppler ultrasound, with parenchymal heterogeneity, is the defining sonographic finding of testicular torsion.

questions.text: What is the definitive treatment of testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: Torsion requires urgent surgical detorsion and orchidopexy (with contralateral fixation), since testicular salvage is entirely time-dependent.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: Urethral discharge suggests urethritis or an STI-related epididymo-orchitis, not torsion; torsion classically presents with sudden pain, a high-riding testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of spermatic cord torsion?
questions.explanation: Prehn's sign (pain relief with testicular elevation) is positive in epididymitis, not torsion — in torsion, elevation does not relieve pain.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about epididymo-orchitis is true?
options: Pain increases when the scrotum is elevated
It is commonly caused by E. coli in sexually active young men
It is typically caused by Chlamydia in a 6-year-old boy
Recurrent epididymo-orchitis may result from a congenital cause
originalOptions: Pain increases when the scrotum is elevated
It is commonly caused by E. coli in sexually active young men
It is typically caused by Chlamydia in a 6-year-old boy
Recurrent epididymo-orchitis may result from a congenital cause
questions.correctAnswer: D) Recurrent epididymo-orchitis may result from a congenital cause
questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent epididymo-orchitis may result from a congenital cause
questions.explanation: Recurrent epididymo-orchitis can result from an underlying congenital abnormality; Prehn's sign (pain relief, not increase, with elevation) favors epididymitis, and Chlamydia/gonorrhea (not E. coli) are typical in sexually active young men, while E. coli predominates in prepubertal boys and older men.

questions.text: A man presents with a palpable right-sided varicocele of 3 months' onset, with no varicocele on the left side. Testis longitudinal axis is 5 cm bilaterally, and semen analysis reveals volume 2.0 mL, density 33 million/mL, and motility 38%. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: An isolated right-sided varicocele is atypical and raises suspicion for a retroperitoneal mass (e.g., RCC) compressing the right testicular vein before it enters the IVC — renal ultrasound is the appropriate initial screening step.

questions.text: A case of an isolated right-sided varicocele. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Renal ultrasound would be the preferred first step if listed; here, CT abdomen is chosen since scrotal ultrasound only confirms the varicocele itself and cannot assess for an underlying retroperitoneal obstructing mass.

questions.text: What are the typical clinical manifestations of varicocele?
questions.explanation: Most varicoceles are asymptomatic, but when symptomatic they can cause chronic testicular heaviness/pain and impaired spermatogenesis leading to infertility.

questions.text: A child presents to the ER with right-sided painful scrotal swelling for 5 hours, an absent cremasteric reflex, and a transverse testicular lie. He ate food 2 hours ago. What is the best management?
options: Wait 4 hours before surgery due to recent food intake
originalOptions: Wait 4 hours before surgery due to recent food intake
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for testicular torsion; surgical exploration must not be delayed for fasting status, since testicular viability is time-dependent.

questions.text: What is the characteristic Doppler ultrasound finding in testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: Decreased or absent intratesticular blood flow on Doppler ultrasound is the hallmark finding confirming torsion.

questions.text: Which sonographic finding is most characteristic of testicular torsion?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Absence of intratesticular blood flow
questions.explanation: Loss of intratesticular blood flow on Doppler ultrasound, along with parenchymal heterogeneity, confirms the diagnosis of torsion.

questions.text: A patient presents with scrotal pain, tenderness, a high-riding testicle, scrotal swelling, and a normal CBC. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation: When the clinical picture is classic for torsion, surgical exploration should not be delayed for imaging, since time to detorsion directly determines testicular salvage.

questions.text: What is the most common age group for testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion peaks around puberty (approximately 12–16 years), commonly attributed to the bell-clapper deformity combined with rapid testicular growth at this age.

questions.text: What are the indications for surgical repair of a varicocele?
questions.explanation: Surgical repair of varicocele is indicated for pain, infertility, or testicular atrophy.

questions.text: A 17-year-old male presents with sudden testicular pain for 5 hours and an absent cremasteric reflex. Doppler ultrasound shows decreased blood flow. What is the next step?
options: Give analgesia, antibiotics, and discharge home
originalOptions: Give analgesia, antibiotics, and discharge home
questions.explanation: The clinical and Doppler findings confirm testicular torsion, which requires immediate surgical exploration and detorsion to salvage the testis.

questions.text: The cremaster muscle is innervated by the:
options: Terminal branches of the subcostal nerve (T12)
Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
originalOptions: Terminal branches of the subcostal nerve (T12)
Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.correctAnswer: D) Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.correctAnswerText: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.explanation: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve is the motor (efferent) limb of the cremasteric reflex, supplying the cremaster muscle.

questions.text: In a sexually active man under 35 years old presenting with epididymitis, which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: In sexually active males aged 14–35 with multiple partners, epididymitis is usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, whereas E. coli is more typical in older men or those with anatomical/functional abnormalities.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sign of testicular torsion?
questions.explanation: An absent cremasteric reflex, along with a high-riding testis and sudden severe pain, is a classic sign of testicular torsion.

questions.text: A 14-year-old boy wakes up at night with sudden onset of severe left testicular pain associated with nausea and vomiting. On examination, the left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. How would this pain most likely be described?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion classically presents with sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting, in contrast to the more insidious onset seen in epididymitis.

questions.text: A young male presents with sudden onset of severe unilateral testicular pain for the past 4 hours. The ultrasound sonographer will not be available for another 4 hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for scrotal Doppler ultrasound before deciding management
Immediate surgical exploration without waiting for imaging
Give analgesia and reassess in 4 hours
originalOptions: Wait for scrotal Doppler ultrasound before deciding management
Immediate surgical exploration without waiting for imaging
Give analgesia and reassess in 4 hours
questions.correctAnswer: B) Immediate surgical exploration without waiting for imaging
questions.correctAnswerText: Immediate surgical exploration without waiting for imaging
questions.explanation: When the clinical picture is classic for testicular torsion, surgical exploration should never be delayed for imaging, since testicular salvage is entirely time-dependent.

questions.text: During scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion, the testis is found to be black and non-viable after detorsion and warm-pack observation. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Leave in place and reassess in 24 hours
originalOptions: Leave in place and reassess in 24 hours
questions.correctAnswer: B) Orchiectomy of the affected testis
questions.explanation: A black, non-viable testis that does not improve in color after detorsion and warm, soaked gauze application should be removed (orchiectomy), followed by fixation of the contralateral testis.

questions.text: A young male presents with acute unilateral scrotal pain. Which of the following are recognized differential diagnoses for acute scrotum? (Select ALL that apply)
options: Referred pain from a ureteral stone
originalOptions: Referred pain from a ureteral stone
questions.correctAnswer: A) Torsion of the testicular appendix / C) Epididymo-orchitis / D) Referred pain from a ureteral stone / E) Complicated inguinoscrotal hernia
questions.correctAnswerText: A) Torsion of the testicular appendix / C) Epididymo-orchitis / D) Referred pain from a ureteral stone / E) Complicated inguinoscrotal hernia
questions.explanation: The differential diagnosis of acute scrotum includes testicular torsion, torsion of the testicular appendix, epididymo-orchitis, trauma, referred pain from a ureteral stone, and a complicated inguinoscrotal hernia.

questions.text: Why is varicocele more commonly left-sided than right-sided?
options: The left testicular artery is longer than the right
The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, with added compression from the nutcracker effect
The right testicular vein has a valve that prevents reflux
The left testis has a higher metabolic rate requiring more venous drainage
originalOptions: The left testicular artery is longer than the right
The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, with added compression from the nutcracker effect
The right testicular vein has a valve that prevents reflux
The left testis has a higher metabolic rate requiring more venous drainage
questions.correctAnswer: B) The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, with added compression from the nutcracker effect
questions.correctAnswerText: The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, with added compression from the nutcracker effect
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle and is compressed between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker effect), raising hydrostatic pressure and causing dilation and tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus; the right testicular vein drains directly into the IVC at an oblique angle.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes a clinical grading of varicocele on physical examination?
questions.explanation: Varicocele is clinically graded as Grade 1 (palpable only with Valsalva), Grade 2 (palpable without Valsalva), and Grade 3 (visible).

questions.text: On scrotal examination, a "bag of worms" texture on palpation of the spermatic cord is most suggestive of which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A "bag of worms" texture on palpation of the spermatic cord, especially with the patient standing, is the classic finding of varicocele due to dilated, tortuous veins of the pampiniform plexus.

questions.text: A large right scrotal swelling is examined as shown below. Which of the following best describes the diagnostic test being performed? [img: hydroceleandtransillumination.png]
questions.explanation: Shining a light source through the scrotal swelling to check for illumination (as shown) is the transillumination test, classically positive in fluid-filled swellings such as hydrocele.

questions.text: A patient presents with the scrotal swelling shown below. Which of the following is a recognized differential diagnosis for this presentation? [img: hydrocelewithouttransillumination.png]
questions.explanation: Scrotal swelling has a broad differential including hydrocele, inguinoscrotal hernia, testicular torsion, and testicular tumor; the correct diagnosis is narrowed down by history, examination (e.g., transillumination), and imaging.

questions.text: A patient presents with the large, non-tender scrotal swelling shown below, which transilluminates with a positive red glow. What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: hydroceleandtransillumination.png]
questions.explanation: A smooth, non-tender scrotal swelling with positive transillumination is classic for hydrocele, a collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis.

questions.text: Regarding the condition shown below, which of the following best defines it? [img: hydrocelewithouttransillumination.png]
options: A collection of serous fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis or along the spermatic cord
A dilatation of the pampiniform plexus veins
A protrusion of bowel through the inguinal canal into the scrotum
A twisting of the spermatic cord compromising testicular blood supply
originalOptions: A collection of serous fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis or along the spermatic cord
A dilatation of the pampiniform plexus veins
A protrusion of bowel through the inguinal canal into the scrotum
A twisting of the spermatic cord compromising testicular blood supply
questions.correctAnswer: A) A collection of serous fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis or along the spermatic cord
questions.correctAnswerText: A collection of serous fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis or along the spermatic cord
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a hydrocele, which may be communicating (patent processus vaginalis) or non-communicating.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized clinical feature of the condition shown below? [img: hydroceleandtransillumination.png]
options: Non-palpable testis due to surrounding fluid
originalOptions: Non-palpable testis due to surrounding fluid
questions.explanation: Hydrocele classically presents with positive transillumination, a non-palpable testis obscured by the surrounding fluid, and absence of tenderness, distinguishing it from more acute or malignant scrotal conditions.

questions.text: A patient presents with the scrotal finding shown below on standing examination. Which of the following best describes this finding? [img: leftvaricocele.png]
options: Visible, dilated, tortuous veins producing a "bag of worms" appearance
Smooth, non-tender swelling with positive transillumination
A high-riding testis with absent cremasteric reflex
A tender, swollen testis with normal skin overlying it
originalOptions: Visible, dilated, tortuous veins producing a "bag of worms" appearance
Smooth, non-tender swelling with positive transillumination
A high-riding testis with absent cremasteric reflex
A tender, swollen testis with normal skin overlying it
questions.correctAnswer: A) Visible, dilated, tortuous veins producing a "bag of worms" appearance
questions.correctAnswerText: Visible, dilated, tortuous veins producing a "bag of worms" appearance
questions.explanation: Visible dilated, tortuous veins without the need for palpation or Valsalva is the classic "bag of worms" appearance of a Grade III varicocele.

questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for the scrotal finding shown below? [img: leftvaricocele.png]
questions.correctAnswer: A) Large left-sided Grade III varicocele
questions.explanation: The visible tortuous "bag of worms" appearance on the left side is diagnostic of a Grade III (visible) varicocele, which is typically left-sided due to the nutcracker effect on the left renal vein.

questions.text: Regarding the condition shown below, which of the following is a recognized indication for surgical repair? [img: leftvaricocele.png]
options: Persistent scrotal pain despite conservative treatment
originalOptions: Persistent scrotal pain despite conservative treatment
questions.explanation: Indications for varicocelectomy include infertility with abnormal semen analysis, testicular atrophy/hypotrophy, and persistent pain unresponsive to conservative measures.

questions.text: BPH most commonly arises from which zone of the prostate?
questions.explanation: BPH develops in the transitional zone, whereas prostate cancer arises predominantly (70–80%) from the peripheral zone.

questions.text: In uncomplicated bladder outflow obstruction due to BPH, which finding is typical?
options: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
originalOptions: Symptom relief with alpha-1 adrenoceptor agonists
Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.correctAnswer: D) Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.correctAnswerText: Voiding flow rate less than 15 mL/sec
questions.explanation: A maximum flow rate below 15 mL/sec (with <10 mL/sec strongly suggestive) is typical of obstruction. Finasteride takes 6+ months to work, and alpha-blockers (not agonists) relieve symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT assessed by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)?
questions.explanation: IPSS assesses seven voiding/storage symptoms (incomplete emptying, frequency, intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, nocturia) but does not include incontinence, As a key word (FUN II SS) frequency,urgency,nocturnal , incomplete empathy,intermittent,stream is weak ,straining

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a symptom of the voiding (obstructive) phase in BPH?
questions.explanation: Frequency is a storage symptom. Voiding/obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, weak stream, straining, intermittency, and terminal dribbling.

questions.text: Which symptom is NOT related to urine storage phase dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Weak stream is a voiding (obstructive) phase symptom. Storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has an IPSS of 22 (severe). What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 blockers such as terazosin are first-line medical therapy for BPH, even with severe IPSS scores. Surgery is reserved for failed medical therapy or complications.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT used in the treatment of BPH?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 agonists cause smooth muscle contraction and would worsen bladder outflow obstruction. Beta-blockers also have no established role in BPH, but alpha-agonists are the classically incorrect option since they directly oppose the mechanism of alpha-blocker therapy.

questions.text: Tamsulosin, used in the treatment of BPH, acts as a(n):
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin is a selective alpha-1A antagonist that relaxes prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle to improve urinary flow.

questions.text: Which of the following is an indication for open (simple) prostatectomy rather than TURP?
options: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
originalOptions: First-line medical therapy failure with small prostate
questions.correctAnswer: A) Prostate size greater than 80 grams
questions.explanation: A prostate weighing more than 80 g is generally too large for safe transurethral resection (increased TUR syndrome risk), making open (or laparoscopic/robotic) simple prostatectomy preferable.

questions.text: Which statement about anticholinergic drugs in BPH is FALSE?
options: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
originalOptions: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
They are used in combination with alpha-blockers
They may cause dry mouth and constipation
questions.correctAnswer: B) They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
questions.correctAnswerText: They are indicated when post-void residual is greater than 150 mL
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics are contraindicated, not indicated, when PVR exceeds 150 mL, due to the risk of precipitating acute urinary retention.

questions.text: Antimuscarinic therapy for LUTS/BPH is contraindicated:
options: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
originalOptions: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
In all men with OAB symptoms
In all men with BPH regardless of PVR
In all men with an enlarged prostate
questions.correctAnswer: A) Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
questions.correctAnswerText: Only in men with large and persistent post-void residual volumes
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinics are contraindicated specifically in men with large, persistent PVR due to retention risk; they can safely be combined with alpha-blockers for mixed storage and voiding symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic medications?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation (not diarrhea), along with dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, and confusion.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized side effect of tamsulosin?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin's known side effects are retrograde ejaculation (most common), postural hypotension, and rhinitis/nasal congestion; decreased libido is not a typical alpha-blocker side effect.

questions.text: Regarding post-void residual (PVR) assessment in BPH, which statement is most accurate?
options: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
originalOptions: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
PVR should always be measured after every single void with volumes over 300 mL
PVR can only be measured by catheterization
PVR has no clinical relevance in BPH management
questions.correctAnswer: A) PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
questions.correctAnswerText: PVR is best assessed by bladder ultrasound, and assessment is important before surgery for related conditions or in patients with voiding symptoms
questions.explanation: PVR is typically measured using ultrasound (avoiding invasive catheterization) and should be assessed in patients with significant voiding symptoms or before certain interventions, though it is not measured after every single void.

questions.text: Which symptom is LEAST specific for bladder outflow obstruction?
questions.explanation: Nocturia can result from many causes (polyuria, cardiac disease, aging) besides bladder outflow obstruction, making it the least specific symptom among the choices.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a storage symptom of BPH?
questions.explanation: Dysuria reflects pain during urination (typically from inflammation) and is not a standard storage LUTS; storage symptoms include frequency, urgency, nocturia, and urge incontinence.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT occur during the voiding phase?
questions.explanation: Nocturia is a storage-phase symptom, while hesitancy and weak stream are voiding-phase symptoms.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with LUTS has IPSS 22 and PVR 50 mL. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.explanation: With a severe IPSS but only mildly elevated PVR and no indication for surgery, first-line medical therapy with an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) is appropriate.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man with BPH has IPSS symptom score of 22, PVR 50 cc, prostate volume 60 cc, severe detrusor instability on cystometrogram, and high-grade obstruction on pressure-flow study. The best next step to improve symptoms is:
questions.explanation: Despite urodynamic evidence of obstruction and detrusor overactivity, initial management remains medical therapy with an alpha-blocker before considering surgery, given no absolute surgical indication is present.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man on tamsulosin and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for 2 months continues to have obstructive symptoms. The next step is:
options: Continue current therapy and reassess later
originalOptions: Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.correctAnswer: B) Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.correctAnswerText: Continue current therapy and reassess later
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors require at least 6 months to show clinical benefit; persistent symptoms after only 3 months, without complications, warrant continued therapy and reassessment rather than surgery.

questions.text: Tamsulosin combined with a PDE5 inhibitor should be used with caution due to the risk of:
questions.explanation: Both alpha-blockers and PDE5 inhibitors cause vasodilation; their combination increases the risk of significant hypotension.

questions.text: Which bladder tumor originates from the urachus?
questions.explanation: Urachal remnants at the bladder dome give rise to adenocarcinoma, often presenting with mucusuria. TCC and SCC arise from urothelium and chronic irritation respectively, not urachal remnants.

questions.text: Which type of bladder cancer is caused due to chronic irritation?
questions.explanation: Chronic irritation (Schistosoma, long-term catheterization, bladder stones, recurrent UTI) causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, progressing to SCC over time.

questions.text: Which of the following environmental factors is highly associated with bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Smoking accounts for roughly half of bladder cancers, conferring a 2–6× increased risk via carcinogenic arylamines. Occupational and radiation exposure are recognized risk factors but contribute far less overall.

questions.text: Typical presentation of bladder cancer:
questions.explanation: This is the classic presentation, seen in 80–85% of patients, and represents total hematuria from the bladder. Irritative symptoms like frequency or dysuria are less common and suggest CIS.

questions.text: 68-year-old male patient diagnosed with bladder TCC; on TURBT histology came back as T2 bladder TCC. Best next treatment option is:i
questions.explanation: T2 disease invades the muscularis propria, defining muscle-invasive bladder cancer, which requires radical cystectomy (± neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy). Intravesical therapies are reserved for non-muscle-invasive disease.

questions.text: Which is considered the best for follow-up of bladder cancer after resection?
questions.explanation: Cystoscopy is the gold standard for surveillance, allowing direct visualization and biopsy of recurrent lesions. Imaging modalities lack the sensitivity to detect small mucosal recurrences.

questions.text: Which one of the following intravesical treatments CANNOT be given immediately after bladder cancer resection?
questions.explanation: Intravesical chemotherapy (such as Mitomycin) can be administered as a single dose within 24 hours of resection to eliminate circulating tumor cells. However, intravesical BCG (an attenuated strain of mycobacteria) must be delayed for at least 2 weeks post-resection. This delay allows the resection site to heal completely, preventing potentially fatal systemic mycobacterial dissemination and BCG-sepsis.

questions.text: High-grade bladder tumor characteristics:
questions.correctAnswer: A) High progression AND high recurrence
questions.explanation: High-grade tumors carry both high recurrence and high progression risk, whereas low-grade tumors have high recurrence but low progression potential.

questions.text: A 62-year-old male presents with intermittent, painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a papillary bladder tumor, and he undergoes a complete transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT). The final histopathology report confirms a Ta, low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the immediate management of this patient?
questions.explanation: A single immediate instillation post-TURBT reduces recurrence by ~50% in Ta low-grade tumors. BCG is reserved for T1, CIS, or high-grade Ta disease due to its higher toxicity.

questions.text: Egyptian man with previous Schistosoma parasite infection — most common bladder cancer type:
questions.explanation: S. haematobium is endemic in Egypt; eggs deposited in the bladder wall trigger chronic inflammation and squamous metaplasia, leading to SCC rather than TCC.

questions.text: Risk factor for bladder cancer from occupation:
questions.explanation: Aromatic amines such as benzidine and beta-naphthylamine are established occupational carcinogens in these industries, as well as in painting and hairdressing.

questions.text: What is the definitive treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion is the gold standard for T2+ disease. Chemotherapy alone and intravesical therapy are inadequate once muscularis propria is invaded.

questions.text: Which group is more affected by bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Male:female ratio is roughly 3:1, with peak incidence at 60–70 years; smoking further amplifies this predominant demographic risk.

questions.text: Which of the following is a risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines in the rubber industry is a well-established, strong risk factor. Family history confers only a modest (two-fold) increase in comparison.

questions.text: Patient with uncontrolled HTN, colon cancer treated with cyclophosphamide + radiotherapy, now has invasive bladder cancer — what is LEAST likely to increase bladder cancer risk?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is not a recognized bladder cancer risk factor, whereas cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiotherapy, and smoking are all established causative agents.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder?
questions.explanation: Eggs lodging in the bladder wall provoke chronic granulomatous inflammation and squamous metaplasia, culminating in SCC — unlike ordinary bacterial UTIs.

questions.text: 60-year-old smoker with painless intermittent gross hematuria. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.correctAnswer: A) TCC (transitional cell carcinoma) bladder cancer
questions.explanation: TCC accounts for ~90% of bladder cancers and is strongly linked to smoking, presenting classically with painless intermittent gross hematuria.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Alcohol has no established causal link to bladder cancer, unlike smoking, occupational carcinogen exposure, and male gender, which are all recognized risk factors.

questions.text: Most common cancer associated with persistent urachus:
questions.explanation: A persistent urachal remnant at the bladder dome predisposes to adenocarcinoma, distinct from the urothelium-derived TCC affecting the rest of the bladder.

questions.text: Patient with bladder cancer stage T1, high risk for progression, underwent resection; after 2 weeks what is the next step?
questions.explanation: High-risk T1 tumors require re-resection (repeat TURBT) to exclude understaging or residual disease before committing to intravesical therapy.

questions.text: Patient treated with BCG has a biopsy showing CIS with muscle invasion. What is the best management?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Radical cystectomy with urinary diversion
questions.explanation: Muscle invasion signifies progression beyond the scope of intravesical therapy; BCG failure with invasive disease mandates radical cystectomy.

questions.text: Patient found to have bladder cancer; after TURBT the histology came back as T1. What is the next step?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Cystoscopy follow-up and intravesical therapy
questions.explanation: T1 tumors are non-muscle-invasive, so management consists of surveillance cystoscopy with intravesical instillation rather than radical surgery.

questions.text: The most common presentation of bladder cancer:
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria is the classic and most common presenting symptom, seen in the majority of bladder cancer patients.

questions.text: Urine cytology is most sensitive for?
options: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
originalOptions: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.correctAnswer: B) High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.correctAnswerText: High-grade bladder cancer and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
questions.explanation: Urine cytology detects poorly differentiated cells shed from high-grade tumors and CIS with high sensitivity, but often misses well-differentiated low-grade lesions.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a component of trimodal therapy for bladder-preserving treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Trimodal therapy combines maximal TURBT with concurrent chemotherapy and radiotherapy specifically to spare the bladder; radical cystectomy is the alternative it aims to avoid.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the classical presentation of bladder cancer, particularly when carcinoma in situ is present?
options: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
originalOptions: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
Flank pain radiating to the groin
questions.correctAnswer: C) Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria
questions.correctAnswerText: Painless intermittent hematuria with urgency, frequency, and dysuria

questions.text: Which chemotherapeutic agent is itself a recognized risk factor for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation: Its urotoxic metabolite (acrolein) damages the urothelium, increasing bladder cancer risk.

questions.text: A low-risk non-muscle-invasive tumor is resected. Most appropriate immediate management?
questions.explanation: A single post-TURBT instillation reduces recurrence in low-risk disease without BCG-level toxicity.

questions.text: A high-risk T1, high-grade tumor is found after TURBT. Recommended intravesical therapy?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Induction BCG followed by maintenance
questions.explanation: High-risk T1/high-grade or CIS requires induction BCG plus maintenance for optimal recurrence/progression control.

questions.text: Which finding after TURBT mandates repeat TURBT?
options: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
originalOptions: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.correctAnswer: B) T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.correctAnswerText: T1 high-grade tumor or incomplete resection
questions.explanation: These carry understaging risk, so repeat TURBT confirms true depth of invasion before further treatment.

questions.text: A patient has very-high-risk or BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. Best management?
questions.explanation: BCG-unresponsive or very-high-risk disease carries high progression risk, favoring cystectomy over further intravesical salvage.

questions.text: Which correctly differentiates timing of chemotherapy vs. BCG after TURBT?
options: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
BCG within 24 hours; chemotherapy delayed 2 weeks
originalOptions: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing

questions.correctAnswerText: Chemotherapy within 24 hours; BCG delayed ≥2 weeks for mucosal healing
questions.explanation: Immediate chemo reduces recurrence; BCG needs intact urothelium to avoid systemic dissemination.

questions.text: An IVU during the bladder-filling phase shows a radiolucent filling defect. Most likely diagnosis? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: A radiolucent filling defect on IVU most commonly represents a urothelial tumor projecting into the lumen.

questions.text: Given a radiolucent bladder filling defect on IVU, which is LEAST likely as a differential? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: Pyelonephritis is a renal parenchymal infection and does not cause a bladder filling defect.

questions.text: A radiolucent bladder filling defect is seen with hematuria. Next step? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]

questions.explanation: TURBT gives histological diagnosis and staging; cytology/imaging are adjuncts, not substitutes.

questions.text: This imaging study was performed during the bladder-filling phase, showing a radiolucent filling defect. What is the name of this imaging study? [img: Intravenousurography.png ]
questions.explanation: IVU uses IV contrast excreted by the kidneys to opacify the collecting system, ureters, and bladder, allowing detection of filling defects such as tumors.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding erectile dysfunction?

The dorsal penile/pudendal nerves carry efferent (motor) fibers arising from S2–S4
Afferent sensory information travels from the penile ischiocavernosus/bulbocavernosus muscles to Onuf's nucleus
A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause
There is no role for checking serum glucose and lipid profile in the evaluation of ED

The dorsal penile/pudendal nerves carry efferent (motor) fibers arising from S2–S4

A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause

questions.correctAnswerText: A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause

questions.text: Tumescence (the erectile phase) is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP and relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, producing tumescence; sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow instead causes detumescence.

questions.text: All of the following are possible causes of non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism EXCEPT:
options: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
originalOptions: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
questions.explanation: Non-ischemic priapism results from an arterio-sinusoidal fistula, classically from trauma, needle injury, or iatrogenic penile surgery; neurologic shock is instead a recognized cause of ischemic (low-flow) priapism.

questions.text: Regarding priapism, which of the following statements is correct?

It is only seen following intracavernosal injections
It is best diagnosed by a plain lateral X-ray of the pelvis
It is more commonly caused by Alprostadil than by Papaverine

questions.explanation: Prolonged ischemic priapism causes progressive corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction if not urgently treated; priapism has many causes besides injections, is diagnosed by aspiration/blood gas and Doppler (not plain X-ray), and shunting is a later, not first-line, option.

questions.text: Which condition is characteristically associated with subcutaneous wire/device erosion through the skin?
questions.explanation: Erosion of the implanted device or its components through the overlying skin is a recognized mechanical complication of penile prosthesis surgery.

questions.text: Which of the following antihypertensive drugs negatively affects erectile function?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide) are reported to cause ED, while alpha-blockers (terazosin) and ARBs (losartan) tend to improve sexual function, and amlodipine/captopril are not associated with worsening erectile function.

questions.text: Which characteristic is typically associated with organic ED, in contrast to psychogenic ED?
options: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
originalOptions: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
questions.correctAnswer: A) Gradual decline in erectile ability
questions.explanation: Organic ED typically has a progressive, gradual course, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved morning/nocturnal erections all favor a psychogenic cause.

questions.text: During a rigid erection, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Dilation of the arterioles and arteries
Subtunical venous compression reducing venous outflow
Corporal pressure rises to several hundred millimeters of mercury
originalOptions: Dilation of the arterioles and arteries

Corporal pressure rises to several hundred millimeters of mercury

questions.explanation: The ischiocavernosus muscles actively contract (not relax) during the rigid erection phase, compressing the crura and driving intracorporal pressure well above systolic blood pressure.

questions.text: A quadriplegic patient presents with priapism. Corporeal blood gas analysis reveals PO2 = 94, PCO2 = 37, pH = 7.4. He was previously treated with intracavernosal phenylephrine without improvement. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.explanation: A near-normal blood gas indicates non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which is managed conservatively and, if intervention is required, by selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or agents used for ischemic priapism.

questions.text: In ischemic priapism, which of the following is typically absent?
questions.explanation: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is characterized by absent or markedly reduced arterial inflow to the cavernosal artery on Doppler, with a painful, fully rigid erection.

questions.text: Which of the following is a psychogenic cause of erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Anxiety acts through overinhibition of the spinal erection center and excessive sympathetic outflow, making it a psychogenic cause, while the other options are organic/structural causes of ED.

questions.text: Pain in the flaccid penis is usually due to:
options: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
originalOptions: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
questions.explanation: Pain in the flaccid penis typically reflects bladder or urethral inflammation (or paraphimosis), whereas Peyronie's disease and priapism classically cause pain in the erect penis.

questions.text: All of the following are characteristics of psychogenic ED EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A gradual, progressive decline in erectile function is characteristic of organic ED, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved nocturnal erections point to a psychogenic cause.

questions.text: What will penile Doppler ultrasound show in a case of ischemic priapism?
options: Increased venous outflow from the corpora
Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
originalOptions: Increased venous outflow from the corpora
Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.correctAnswer: D) Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.correctAnswerText: Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.explanation: Ischemic priapism is a low-flow state, so Doppler characteristically shows absent or minimal arterial inflow into the cavernosal artery.

questions.text: A patient presents with priapism of 2 weeks' duration; corporeal blood gas shows PO2 > 90, PCO2 < 30. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: A high PO2 and low PCO2 indicate non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which, when intervention is required, is managed with selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or sympathomimetic injection, which are used for ischemic priapism.

questions.text: An 80-year-old paraplegic man develops a prolonged, painful erection after an intracorporeal injection given to treat erectile dysfunction. Which intracorporeal drug should be given to relieve him?
questions.explanation: This describes ischemic priapism following intracavernosal injection therapy, which is treated with aspiration/irrigation followed by intracavernosal phenylephrine (an alpha-agonist); alprostadil, papaverine, and sildenafil are used to induce erection, not to treat priapism.

questions.text: A 38-year-old paraplegic man develops a sustained erection lasting 10 hours following intracorporeal injection of 10 mcg of prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil). What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: This is drug-induced ischemic priapism, which is treated with corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine, an alpha-agonist that induces vasoconstriction and detumescence.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors is TRUE?
options: Sildenafil has efficacy maintained for approximately 4–6 hours
They increase the cytoplasmic concentration of cAMP
They can be safely combined with nitrates
Tadalafil has a shorter duration of action than sildenafil

questions.correctAnswerText: Sildenafil has efficacy maintained for approximately 4–6 hours
questions.explanation: Sildenafil and vardenafil act within 30–60 minutes with efficacy maintained for about 4–6 hours, unlike tadalafil which lasts up to 36 hours; PDE5 inhibitors raise cGMP (not cAMP) and are contraindicated with nitrates.

questions.text: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors increase the cytoplasmic concentration of:
questions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors block the breakdown of cGMP by phosphodiesterase type 5, prolonging cGMP-mediated cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.text: An elderly patient on nitroglycerin presents with erectile dysfunction. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate use due to the risk of severe hypotension, so a non-pharmacologic option such as a vacuum erection device is appropriate; testosterone and tamsulosin are not indicated without evidence of hypogonadism or BPH.

questions.text: All of the following favor a diagnosis of organic (rather than psychogenic) erectile dysfunction EXCEPT:

questions.correctAnswerText: Arteriogenic ED — decreased peak systolic velocity; Venogenic ED — persistent end-diastolic flow
questions.explanation: Arteriogenic ED reflects reduced arterial inflow, shown as a low peak systolic velocity, while venogenic ED reflects failure of veno-occlusion, shown as persistent end-diastolic flow despite adequate inflow.

questions.text: Which of the following is correct? [img: ABtrue.png]

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized hormonal cause of erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Both hypogonadism (low testosterone) and hyperprolactinemia are established hormonal causes of ED; hyperprolactinemia additionally suppresses GnRH, which further lowers testosterone.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of PDE5 inhibitors in the treatment of erectile dysfunction?
options: They increase cAMP by inhibiting adenylate cyclase breakdown

They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
They block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the prostate and bladder neck

questions.explanation: Sexual stimulation triggers NO release, raising cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors block the enzyme that degrades cGMP, thereby prolonging smooth muscle relaxation and erection — they require intact sexual stimulation and do not act independently.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding contraindications and adverse effects of PDE5 inhibitors EXCEPT:

questions.text: Regarding drug-specific adverse effects of PDE5 inhibitors, which of the following is correct? [img: ABtruePDE5.png]

questions.correctAnswerText: A persistent penile erection unrelated to sexual stimulation that fails to subside

questions.explanation: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is classically caused by sickle cell disease and vasoactive/intracavernosal drugs, while non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism results from blunt perineal or penile trauma causing a cavernosal arterial injury (arteriocavernosal fistula).

questions.text: All of the following are true differences between ischemic and non-ischemic priapism EXCEPT:

questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies two intracavernosal drugs used for erectile dysfunction and a shared major adverse effect?

questions.text: Regarding urological imaging studies, what is the most important risk of exposure to ionizing radiation?
questions.explanation: Ionizing radiation from CT and fluoroscopic urological studies carries a cumulative risk of carcinogenesis, making malignancy induction the most clinically significant long-term hazard. questions.text: The correct order of the division of the intrarenal branches of the renal artery is:
questions.explanation: The renal artery branches sequentially from segmental arteries into interlobar arteries running between pyramids, then arcuate arteries arching at the corticomedullary junction, and finally interlobular arteries ascending into the cortex.

questions.text: Which of the following is associated with suprapubic pain?
questions.explanation: Bladder pathology such as cystitis or overdistension classically produces suprapubic discomfort, whereas renal colic and ureteric stones typically cause flank pain radiating to the groin.

questions.text: All the following can cause a DECREASE in specific gravity of urine EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dehydration concentrates the urine, raising specific gravity, whereas increased fluid intake, diuretics, and impaired concentrating ability all dilute urine and lower specific gravity.

questions.text: Which of the following are used in the calculation of plasma osmolarity?
questions.explanation: Plasma osmolarity is estimated as 2×Na + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, incorporating sodium as the main osmotic contributor along with glucose and urea.

options: Inflamed kidney causes colicky pain and obstruction causes steady pain
Obstruction causes colicky pain and inflammation causes steady pain
Renal colic fluctuates in intensity as the kidney attempts to relieve obstruction
Steady inflammatory pain reflects capsular distension without peristaltic surges
Obstructive pain fluctuates due to ureteral peristalsis against the blockage

questions.text: Radiographically, the ureter is divided into how many parts?
questions.explanation: The ureter is anatomically and radiologically divided into upper, middle (over the sacrum), and lower segments, corresponding to abdominal, pelvic, and intramural portions.

questions.text: Which of the following drugs does NOT cause renal failure?
questions.explanation: Tamsulosin is an alpha-blocker used for bladder outlet obstruction and lacks nephrotoxic potential, unlike ACE inhibitors, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, and NSAIDs, which can impair renal perfusion or cause direct tubular injury.

questions.text: Which imaging modality is safest for a patient in renal failure?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound requires no contrast or radiation exposure and is unaffected by renal function, making it the safest imaging choice in renal impairment, unlike iodinated or gadolinium-based contrast studies which risk nephrotoxicity or nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

questions.text: Renal pain classically radiates to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain radiates from the flank toward the groin and may be referred to the testis due to shared T11-T12 innervation, distinguishing it from intraperitoneal pain, which classically radiates to the shoulder.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the male urethra from proximal to distal?
questions.explanation: The male urethra begins at the bladder neck, passing through the prostatic segment, then the membranous urethra at the external sphincter, followed by the bulbar and pendulous penile urethra ending at the fossa navicularis.

questions.text: A patient presents with flank pain. Which feature would favor a urological (renal) rather than an intraperitoneal cause?
options: Pain is steady and patient lies motionless
Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs

Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
Pain is aggravated by movement and relieved by lying still
Pain is associated with peritoneal signs
questions.correctAnswer: C) Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
questions.correctAnswerText: Patient prefers to move around and roll to find comfort
questions.explanation: Renal colic patients characteristically move restlessly (rolling sign) due to colicky pain, whereas intraperitoneal pathology causes steady pain with patients preferring to remain motionless.

questions.text: Pneumaturia is best defined as which of the following?

Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine

Involuntary loss of urine during sleep
Presence of blood in the urine
Presence of protein in the urine

questions.explanation: Pneumaturia results from recent catheterization, an enteric fistula, or infection with gas-forming organisms, distinguishing it from hematuria (blood) or enuresis (nocturnal incontinence).

The left gonadal vein terminates directly in the inferior vena cava

Varicocele is more common on the left side than the right

questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation presents with new-onset gross hematuria and mild flank discomfort, with no fever or dysuria. What is the best initial investigation?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation and contrast, making it the safest first-line imaging choice in pregnancy for evaluating hematuria.

questions.text: One of the following is true about the prostate:
options: It secretes the majority of seminal fluid volume
originalOptions: It secretes the majority of seminal fluid volume
questions.explanation: A is correct — the prostate secretes zinc, citric acid, and PSA. B is wrong because fructose is a seminal vesicle product. C is wrong; albumin is not a prostatic secretion. D is wrong because the seminal vesicles, not the prostate, contribute the majority of seminal fluid volume. E is wrong; testosterone is produced by the testis, not the prostate.

questions.text: In a 30-year-old patient with microscopic hematuria confirmed on two consecutive urinalyses, which combination correctly represents the essential investigations and the causes of hematuria to consider?

questions.correctAnswerText: Essential investigations: cystoscopy and upper tract imaging; Causes: urinary tract stones, urothelial/renal malignancy, glomerular disease
questions.explanation: Hematuria in an adult is malignancy until proven otherwise, so cystoscopy assesses the bladder while upper tract imaging evaluates the kidneys and ureters, with stones, malignancy, and glomerular disease as the key causes to exclude. The distractors instead describe irritative symptom workup, scrotal pathology, or bladder outlet obstruction assessment, none of which target hematuria evaluation.

questions.text: All of the following are appropriate questions to ask when taking a history of hematuria EXCEPT:
options: Is the blood present at the start, throughout, or at the end of the urinary stream?
Is the hematuria associated with pain, or is it painless?
Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?

Are there any visible blood clots, and if so, what shape are they?
Is there a history of smoking or occupational exposure to dyes or chemicals?
Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.correctAnswer: E) Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.correctAnswerText: Does the patient experience morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes?
questions.explanation: Timing of blood in the stream, presence or absence of pain, clot characteristics, and smoking or occupational exposure history are all directly relevant to localizing and risk-stratifying hematuria, whereas morning stiffness is a rheumatological question unrelated to urological assessment.

questions.text: All of the following are irritative LUTS symptoms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hesitancy is an obstructive symptom reflecting delayed initiation of urination, whereas frequency, urgency, nocturia, and dysuria are all irritative symptoms related to bladder storage and mucosal irritation.

questions.text: A 68-year-old man reports voiding 10 times during the day and waking up 3 times at night to urinate, each time passing only a small volume, with a strong sudden desire to void that is difficult to defer. His total 24-hour urine output is normal. Which category of symptoms best describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: Frequency, nocturia with small voided volumes, and urgency despite a normal total daily urine output point to decreased functional bladder capacity or mucosal irritation, characteristic of irritative rather than obstructive symptoms.

questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes true hematuria from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: Dipstick is positive for blood in all three conditions, but only true hematuria shows intact red blood cells on microscopic urinalysis.

questions.text: A patient reports blood appearing only at the very end of the urinary stream, after most of the urine has already passed. This pattern of terminal hematuria most suggests pathology arising from:
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bladder neck or prostatic inflammation
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria localizes to the urethra, total hematuria to the bladder or upper tract, and terminal hematuria to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra.

questions.text: A 68-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless gross hematuria. Which diagnosis must be excluded first as the classic cause of painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 years old?
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, warranting cystoscopy and upper tract imaging regardless of other findings.

questions.text: A normotensive patient is found to have isolated microscopic hematuria on routine urinalysis, with no other urinary symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate initial action?
questions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria in a low-risk patient is initially managed conservatively with a repeat urinalysis rather than immediate invasive workup.

questions.text: When taking a history from a patient presenting with hematuria, which combination of questions is most important to ask?
questions.explanation: Onset, presence of clots, and timing during the urinary stream all help localize the source and severity of hematuria, so all should be asked.

questions.text: Hematuria in an adult should be treated as a warning sign of which of the following until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Although hematuria has many causes, it is classically taught that hematuria in an adult signals malignancy, most often bladder cancer, until excluded.

questions.text: A 70-year-old male smoker presents with gross hematuria persisting for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
questions.explanation: Persistent gross hematuria in an older smoker requires full evaluation of both the upper tract (CT urogram) and lower tract (cystoscopy) to exclude urothelial malignancy.

questions.text: Which of the following best defines stress urinary incontinence?
options: Involuntary leakage preceded by a sudden urge to void
Continuous leakage of urine unrelated to activity
Leakage of urine that occurs only during sleep
Leakage of urine following bladder overdistension
Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
originalOptions: Involuntary leakage preceded by a sudden urge to void
Continuous leakage of urine unrelated to activity
Leakage of urine that occurs only during sleep
Leakage of urine following bladder overdistension
Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.correctAnswer: E) Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.correctAnswerText: Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.explanation: Stress incontinence occurs when rises in intra-abdominal pressure overcome urethral resistance, typically from pelvic floor weakness or sphincteric incompetence.

questions.text: A patient with overactive bladder and urgency incontinence is being started on treatment. Which type of incontinence is most often managed pharmacologically as first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity responds well to antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron), unlike stress incontinence, which is managed primarily with conservative or surgical measures.

questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with urine leakage on coughing and sneezing. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Conservative pelvic floor exercises (at least 8 contractions, 3 times daily for 3 months) are first-line before considering surgical options such as slings or Burch colposuspension.

questions.text: A 43-year-old woman develops constant urinary leakage 7 days after hysterectomy, not aggravated by coughing and without associated urgency. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Continuous, position-independent leakage after pelvic surgery strongly suggests an iatrogenic vesicovaginal fistula creating a direct communication between bladder and vagina.

questions.text: Continuous incontinence, defined as leakage of urine at all times and in all positions, is most commonly caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: A fistulous communication between the bladder and vagina bypasses the normal continence mechanism entirely, producing constant leakage regardless of posture or activity.

questions.text: In female patients, an ectopic ureter classically causes continuous urinary incontinence because the ureter inserts:
options: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
originalOptions: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.correctAnswerText: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.explanation: In females, an ectopic ureter frequently opens below the external sphincter, bypassing continence mechanisms; in males it opens above the sphincter and instead causes recurrent UTIs rather than incontinence.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a risk factor for urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: Female sex, not male sex, is a recognized risk factor for urinary incontinence due to a shorter urethra and the effects of pregnancy and childbirth on pelvic floor support.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor specifically for stress urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: Vaginal childbirth weakens pelvic floor support and increases SUI risk, whereas nulliparous women have a comparatively lower risk.

questions.text: Which class of medication should be avoided when treating stress urinary incontinence in a male patient?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics target detrusor overactivity in urge incontinence and have no role in stress incontinence, which in men is usually secondary to sphincter injury after prostate surgery.

questions.text: What is the most common overall indication for placement of an indwelling Foley catheter?
options: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
originalOptions: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.correctAnswer: B) Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.correctAnswerText: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.explanation: Drainage of acute or chronic retention (or post-void residual) is the most common indication for catheterization; monitoring urine output is the second most common.

questions.text: A patient started on an antimuscarinic for urge incontinence develops several adverse effects. Which of the following is NOT typically caused by anticholinergic medications?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and confusion.

questions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for urge incontinence, which of the following should prompt the greatest caution or avoidance of therapy?
questions.explanation: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so severe uncontrolled hypertension is a major safety concern, whereas significant urinary retention with high PVR is a relative caution rather than the primary contraindication.

questions.text: During cystometry, a patient's intravesical pressure (Pves) is 45 cmH2O and abdominal pressure (Pabd) is 15 cmH2O. What is the calculated detrusor pressure (Pdet)?
questions.explanation: Detrusor pressure is calculated as Pdet = Pves − Pabd, so 45 − 15 = 30 cmH2O.

questions.text: A 6-year-old child is undergoing urodynamic evaluation. Using the standard pediatric formula, what is the expected bladder capacity?
questions.explanation: Pediatric bladder capacity is estimated as (Age + 2) × 30 mL; for a 6-year-old this is (6+2) × 30 = 240 mL.

questions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for the treatment of urge urinary incontinence, which of the following conditions is the most appropriate reason to avoid or use the drug with significant caution?
options: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
originalOptions: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.correctAnswer: B) Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.correctAnswerText: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.explanation: Mirabegron (a β3-adrenergic agonist) relaxes the detrusor muscle during bladder filling, which may worsen pre-existing urinary retention. Therefore, patients with significant urinary retention and a high post-void residual should generally avoid the drug or receive it only with careful monitoring. Dysuria, kidney stones, and hematuria are not contraindications by themselves.

questions.text: Which of the following syndromes represents the most common chromosomal cause of male infertility?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing male infertility by leading to primary testicular failure and azoospermia, whereas Kallmann syndrome is a genetic hormone disorder (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) rather than a chromosomal aneuploidy, Turner syndrome exclusively affects females (45,X), and Noonan syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition not characterized by a chromosomal number defect.

questions.text: What is the first-line investigation of choice for a male presenting with infertility?
questions.explanation: Semen analysis (seminal fluid analysis) is the first-line investigation in male infertility, assessing volume, sperm concentration, motility, and morphology; hormonal testing, ultrasound, and karyotyping are reserved for further work-up based on initial findings.

questions.text: Infertility in males with cystic fibrosis is most commonly caused by which of the following?
options: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
originalOptions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.correctAnswer: B) Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.explanation: CFTR gene mutations in cystic fibrosis lead to CBAVD; spermatogenesis is normal, but the resulting obstructive azoospermia causes infertility.

questions.text: Which of the following is the primary inhibitor of LH release from the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: Testosterone provides negative feedback on both the hypothalamus (↓GnRH) and pituitary (↓LH). Inhibin B, secreted by Sertoli cells, selectively inhibits FSH rather than LH.

questions.text: Oligospermia is best defined as:
options: Complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate
A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold
An abnormal percentage of sperm forms on morphology

A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold

questions.correctAnswer: C) A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold
questions.correctAnswerText: A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold
questions.explanation: Oligospermia: sperm count less than 15 x10⁶/mL , A: Asthenospermia , B: Azoospermia , D: Teratospermia .

questions.text: Teratospermia refers to which of the following semen abnormalities?
options: Absence of sperm in the ejaculate
originalOptions: Absence of sperm in the ejaculate
questions.explanation: Teratospermia: sperm morphology below the lower reference limit of normal forms (WHO lower limit ~4% normal forms) , A: Azoospermia , B: Asthenospermia , C: Oligospermia .

questions.text: The majority of seminal fluid volume is contributed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles contribute the majority of seminal fluid volume, while the prostate contributes about 1/6, and sperm contribute only about 1%.

questions.text: At which life stages do the major physiological peaks of testosterone production occur in males?
options: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
originalOptions: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.correctAnswer: D) Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.correctAnswerText: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.explanation: Testosterone peaks at three distinct life stages: embryonic development, the first few months of neonatal life (mini-puberty), and puberty — driving prostatic and genital development at each stage.

questions.text: A young male bodybuilder using exogenous testosterone is most likely to experience which effect on his fertility?
options: Increased fertility due to higher androgen levels
Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
Fertility effects depend only on the route of administration
originalOptions: Increased fertility due to higher androgen levels
Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
Fertility effects depend only on the route of administration
questions.correctAnswer: B) Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
questions.correctAnswerText: Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
questions.explanation: Exogenous testosterone suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary GnRH/FSH/LH secretion via negative feedback, lowering intratesticular testosterone and impairing spermatogenesis, unlike endogenous testicular testosterone.

questions.text: A patient presents with infertility, small testes, azoospermia, and an elevated FSH level. This clinical picture is most consistent with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Small testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH indicate primary testicular failure (which is synonymous with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) ; hypogonadotropic hypogonadism instead presents with low FSH/LH , and obstructive azoospermia typically has a normal FSH.

questions.text: In a patient with azoospermia, which hormone finding suggests an obstructive cause rather than testicular failure?
questions.explanation: Obstructive azoospermia typically shows a normal FSH because spermatogenesis is intact, whereas non-obstructive azoospermia (testicular failure) shows an elevated FSH due to loss of Sertoli cell inhibin feedback.

questions.text: The anatomical basis of the blood-testis barrier is formed by which of the following?
options: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
originalOptions: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.correctAnswer: B) Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.correctAnswerText: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells are linked by tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier, creating an immunologically privileged compartment for developing sperm, which form only after puberty.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized complication of cryptorchidism?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism impairs fertility due to an unfavorable thermal environment for spermatogenesis; it also raises the risk of testicular (not bladder) cancer.

questions.text: What is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is caused by an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), resulting in small firm testes, gynecomastia, tall stature, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with infertility.

questions.text: Infertility is defined as the failure of a couple to achieve pregnancy after which duration of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse?
questions.explanation: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse; shorter periods (3–6 months) are not sufficient to establish the diagnosis since most couples conceive within a year.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs correctly represents the prevalence of varicocele in the general male population versus in infertile men?
questions.explanation: Varicocele affects about 15% of the general male population but is found in roughly 35–40% of infertile men, and is even more common in men with secondary infertility.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a favorable prognostic factor in male infertility?
options: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
originalOptions: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
questions.explanation: A shorter duration of infertility, younger female partner age, and a history of previous conception are all favorable prognostic factors; the opposite findings (long duration, older maternal age, no prior pregnancy) indicate a poorer prognosis.

questions.text: All of the following are recognized categories of causes of male infertility EXCEPT:
options: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
originalOptions: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.correctAnswer: E) Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.correctAnswerText: Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.explanation: Male infertility is classified into pre-testicular, testicular, post-testicular, and idiopathic causes; a purely psychological category unrelated to organic pathology is not part of this recognized classification.

questions.text: All of the following are recognized causes of obstructive azoospermia EXCEPT:
options: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
originalOptions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.explanation: CBAVD, vasectomy, post-infectious epididymal obstruction, and ejaculatory duct obstruction are classic causes of obstructive azoospermia with preserved spermatogenesis; Klinefelter syndrome causes non-obstructive (testicular failure) azoospermia due to primary testicular failure, not obstruction.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding semen fluid analysis in obstructive azoospermia is correct?
options: Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with usually normal semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction specifically shows low volume with acidic, low-fructose semen
Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with low semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction shows normal volume with normal fructose
Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show low semen volume and low fructose
Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show normal semen volume and normal fructose
Obstructive azoospermia is always associated with elevated FSH regardless of the level of obstruction
originalOptions: Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with usually normal semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction specifically shows low volume with acidic, low-fructose semen
Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with low semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction shows normal volume with normal fructose
Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show low semen volume and low fructose
Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show normal semen volume and normal fructose
Obstructive azoospermia is always associated with elevated FSH regardless of the level of obstruction
questions.correctAnswer: A) Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with usually normal semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction specifically shows low volume with acidic, low-fructose semen
