questions.correctAnswerText: Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with usually normal semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction specifically shows low volume with acidic, low-fructose semen
questions.explanation: In general, obstructive azoospermia preserves normal ejaculate volume since spermatogenesis is intact; however, ejaculatory duct obstruction or absent seminal vesicles is an important exception producing low-volume, acidic, low-fructose semen, and FSH remains normal since testicular function is preserved.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs represents andrological conditions correctly associated with varicocele?
questions.explanation: Varicocele is classically associated with male infertility (abnormal semen parameters) and testicular hypotrophy/atrophy due to impaired thermoregulation and venous stasis; the other listed pairings are unrelated conditions not causally linked to varicocele.

questions.text: A young infertile male undergoes karyotype analysis. Which of the following is the most common genetic cause of male infertility?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common sex chromosome abnormality and genetic cause of male infertility, presenting with small firm testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH/LH with low testosterone.

questions.text: Which statement about carcinoma of the prostate is correct?
options: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
originalOptions: It is typically a squamous cell carcinoma
It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
It is not influenced by hormone manipulation
It commonly invades the rectum directly
It occurs predominantly in the central zone
questions.correctAnswer: B) It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
questions.correctAnswerText: It is graded histologically using the Gleason score
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer is an adenocarcinoma graded by the Gleason score, arises predominantly in the peripheral zone, is hormone-dependent (responds to androgen deprivation therapy), and rarely invades the rectum due to Denonvilliers' fascia.

questions.text: What grading system is used for prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: The Gleason score assesses glandular architecture on low-power microscopy and correlates with prognosis; Bloom-Richardson is used for breast cancer, Breslow for melanoma, and Fuhrman for renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: PSA density is calculated as:
options: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
originalOptions: Free PSA divided by total PSA
Total PSA multiplied by prostate volume
Free PSA divided by prostate volume
Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
Total PSA divided by patient age
questions.correctAnswer: D) Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
questions.correctAnswerText: Total PSA divided by total prostate volume
questions.explanation: PSA density is total serum PSA divided by prostate volume (measured by TRUS); values above 0.15 ng/mL/g raise suspicion for malignancy.

questions.text: Serum PSA and digital rectal examination are primarily used for:
questions.correctAnswer: B) Early detection/screening for prostate cancer
questions.explanation: PSA testing combined with DRE is used for early detection of prostate cancer in asymptomatic men, though PSA is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific.

questions.text: Watchful waiting (as opposed to active surveillance) is most appropriate for men who:
options: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
originalOptions: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
Have impalpable cancer not visible on imaging
questions.correctAnswer: C) Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
questions.correctAnswerText: Have a life expectancy of 10 years or less with well-to-moderately differentiated cancer
questions.explanation: Watchful waiting is a palliative, symptom-directed strategy reserved for patients with limited life expectancy (≤10 years) and less aggressive disease, distinct from active surveillance which is used in younger, low-risk patients with curative intent.

questions.text: The most common site of prostate cancer metastasis is:
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer classically metastasizes to the axial skeleton, particularly the lumbar spine, producing osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions with associated back pain and elevated alkaline phosphatase.

questions.text: Which statement about the Gleason grading system is FALSE?
options: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
originalOptions: It is commonly used for prostate cancer
It does not correlate with prognosis
A higher score indicates worse prognosis
questions.correctAnswer: C) It does not correlate with prognosis
questions.correctAnswerText: It does not correlate with prognosis
questions.explanation: This statement is false — the Gleason score strongly correlates with prognosis and guides management decisions in prostate cancer.

questions.text: Serum PSA elevation may occur in association with which of the following?
questions.explanation: PSA is organ-specific, not disease-specific, and can be elevated by BPH, prostatitis, cancer, and mechanical manipulation of the prostate (e.g., catheterization, biopsy, DRE).

questions.text: Which is the most common cancer diagnosed in urology?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer diagnosed in men overall and the most common urological malignancy.

questions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has a Gleason score of 8 and PSA 25. Which of the following is NOT an appropriate management option?
questions.explanation: Active surveillance is reserved for low-risk disease; a Gleason score of 8 with PSA 25 indicates high-risk disease requiring definitive treatment such as surgery or radiotherapy with hormonal therapy.

questions.text: A patient with Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer is best managed with:
questions.explanation: Gleason 3+3 (grade group 1) represents low-risk disease, for which active surveillance is generally preferred to avoid overtreatment, provided other risk factors (PSA, stage, patient preference) support this approach.

questions.text: A patient has a suspicious prostatic mass on digital rectal exam with PSA of 9 ng/mL. The next step is:
questions.explanation: A suspicious DRE finding combined with elevated PSA warrants histological diagnosis via ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy rather than proceeding directly to surveillance or watchful waiting.

questions.text: All of the following are indications for prostate biopsy EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A high free:total PSA ratio (such as 30%) is reassuring and associated with a lower likelihood of cancer; a low ratio would instead raise suspicion and support biopsy.

questions.text: The Gleason score is used specifically for grading:
questions.explanation: The Gleason score is a histological grading system exclusively for prostate adenocarcinoma, based on glandular differentiation patterns.

questions.text: A patient with known advanced prostate cancer presents with new-onset back pain. The most appropriate immediate step is:
options: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
originalOptions: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.correctAnswer: D) Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent assessment for spinal metastasis/cord compression, then consideration of androgen-deprivation therapy
questions.explanation: New back pain in a patient with known prostate cancer must first be evaluated for vertebral metastasis or spinal cord compression as an oncologic emergency; systemic androgen-deprivation therapy (GnRH/LHRH agonist) is appropriate for the underlying metastatic disease once red flags are excluded.

questions.text: A patient with prostate cancer has Gleason grade 8 and PSA greater than 20 with no metastatic findings on staging. Which management option is NOT appropriate?
questions.explanation: Active surveillance is unsuitable for high-risk, non-metastatic disease (Gleason 8, PSA >20); definitive treatment with surgery or radiotherapy plus hormonal therapy is indicated.

questions.text: After one year of therapy with a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, PSA typically:
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors reduce PSA levels by approximately 50% after 6–12 months of therapy; this must be accounted for when interpreting PSA values in patients on these drugs.

questions.text: What is the most common presentation of renal cell carcinoma?
options: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
originalOptions: Classic triad of hematuria, pain, and mass
questions.explanation: Most RCCs are now discovered incidentally on imaging performed for unrelated reasons; the classic triad occurs in fewer than 10% of cases.

questions.text: What is the most common histopathological subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Clear cell RCC accounts for approximately 75% of RCC cases, is associated with VHL gene mutations, and carries the worst prognosis among the common subtypes.

questions.text: The most common paraneoplastic syndrome associated with RCC is:
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia, mediated via PTHrP secretion, is the most common paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with 2 months of painless visible hematuria, hypertension, weight loss, low-grade fever, and anemia. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Painless visible hematuria with hypertension and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fever, anemia) reflects the paraneoplastic and systemic presentation classically associated with renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: Renal cell carcinoma is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A vegetarian diet is not an established risk factor for RCC; recognized risk factors include smoking, obesity, hypertension, long-term dialysis (ESRD), and inherited syndromes such as VHL disease.

questions.text: A patient presents with pneumothorax, cutaneous fibrofolliculomas, and a renal tumor. The most likely RCC subtype is:
questions.explanation: This triad is characteristic of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, which is associated with chromophobe/oncocytic renal tumors, skin fibrofolliculomas, and pulmonary cysts predisposing to pneumothorax.

questions.text: A patient has an RCC measuring 4 cm confined to the kidney. The preferred treatment is:
questions.explanation: Partial nephrectomy is preferred for T1 tumors (≤7 cm) when technically feasible, as it provides equivalent oncologic outcomes to radical nephrectomy while preserving renal function.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized paraneoplastic manifestation of RCC?
questions.explanation: Increased serotonin is not a recognized paraneoplastic feature of RCC; recognized paraneoplastic syndromes include erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia, hypertension, and Stauffer's syndrome (hepatic dysfunction without metastases).

questions.text: A fat-containing renal mass identified on ultrasound is most likely:
questions.explanation: Macroscopic fat within a renal mass is pathognomonic for angiomyolipoma, a benign tumor composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat.

questions.text: The classic triad of renal cell carcinoma consists of:
options: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
originalOptions: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.correctAnswer: D) Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.correctAnswerText: Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass
questions.explanation: The classic (but now uncommon) triad of RCC is hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable flank mass, occurring together in less than 10% of patients.

questions.text: The most common site of RCC metastasis is:
questions.explanation: The lung is the most common site of metastasis for renal cell carcinoma, followed by bone and liver.

questions.text: Which of the following is an established risk factor for renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Hypertension is a well-established risk factor for RCC, along with smoking, obesity, and long-term dialysis; alcohol and diabetes are not classically listed among the primary risk factors.

questions.text: Most cases of renal cell carcinoma are discovered:
questions.explanation: The majority of RCCs are detected incidentally during imaging performed for unrelated indications, reflecting the often silent early course of the disease.

questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents with hypotension, flank pain, and Cullen and Grey Turner signs, with no prior similar episodes. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage from a ruptured angiomyolipoma (Wunderlich syndrome) can present with flank pain, hypotension, and flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner sign), and is more likely to occur or become symptomatic during pregnancy.

questions.text: A patient with RCC presents with elevated hemoglobin (erythrocytosis). Which hormone is responsible?
questions.explanation: Ectopic erythropoietin secretion by the tumor causes paraneoplastic erythrocytosis in RCC; PTHrP causes hypercalcemia, not erythrocytosis.

questions.text: A 42-year-old Black male with known sickle cell disease is diagnosed with RCC. The most likely subtype is:
questions.explanation: Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait/disease and typically occurs in young Black patients, distinguishing it from the other subtypes.

questions.text: A patient is found to have a solid 4x5 cm renal mass in the lower pole. The next step in evaluation is:
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the gold standard for characterizing a solid renal mass, as it allows assessment of enhancement (the key feature distinguishing RCC from benign lesions) and staging.

questions.text: A key imaging characteristic of tumors associated with Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is:
questions.explanation: VHL-associated clear cell RCC tumors are characteristically hypervascular due to upregulation of angiogenic factors from loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene.

questions.text: Which of the following are established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma?
options: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
originalOptions: Vegetarian diet and low salt intake
questions.explanation: ESRD, Smoking, obesity, and hypertension are all recognized, established risk factors for renal cell carcinoma.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized paraneoplastic syndrome in RCC?
questions.explanation: Polycythemia (erythrocytosis) due to ectopic erythropoietin secretion is a well-recognized paraneoplastic syndrome of RCC; RCC is in fact the most common cause of paraneoplastic erythrocytosis

questions.text: Regarding the composition of urinary calculi, what is the most common stone type?
questions.explanation: Calcium oxalate stones account for approximately 80% of all urinary calculi, making them by far the most common type.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding kidney stones is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Kidney stones are actually 2–3 times more common in males, not females, which makes this statement false.

questions.text: Regarding uric acid calculi, which of the following is correct?
options: Occur less frequently after treatment with penicillamine
Are typically well demonstrated by CT scan
Can be dissolved by treatment with allopurinol
Are the most common upper tract calculi
originalOptions: Occur less frequently after treatment with penicillamine
Are typically well demonstrated by CT scan
Can be dissolved by treatment with allopurinol
Are the most common upper tract calculi
questions.correctAnswer: B) Are typically well demonstrated by CT scan
questions.correctAnswerText: Are typically well demonstrated by CT scan
questions.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain KUB but are well visualized on non-contrast CT, which detects virtually all stone types.

questions.text: A patient presents with a urinary stone associated with fever, WBC count of 18,000, hydronephrosis, and abnormal creatinine. What is the best next step in management?
options: Admit with JJ stent or nephrostomy
originalOptions: Admit with JJ stent or nephrostomy
questions.correctAnswer: D) Admit with JJ stent or nephrostomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Admit with JJ stent or nephrostomy
questions.explanation: An obstructed, infected kidney (fever, leukocytosis, hydronephrosis, renal impairment) is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression with a JJ stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, not conservative management.

questions.text: The most important factor in the formation of uric acid calculi is:
options: Limited solubility of uric acid in acidic solution
Concentration of uric acid in the urine
originalOptions: Limited solubility of uric acid in acidic solution
Concentration of uric acid in the urine
questions.correctAnswer: A) Limited solubility of uric acid in acidic solution
questions.correctAnswerText: Limited solubility of uric acid in acidic solution
questions.explanation: Low urinary pH is the critical determinant of uric acid stone formation, since uric acid is poorly soluble in acidic urine regardless of the other listed factors.

questions.text: A 75-year-old woman being investigated for recurrent UTIs (Proteus on culture) has a staghorn calculus on CT. What is the most likely stone composition?
questions.explanation: Proteus produces urease, which splits urea into ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and favoring precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones, classically forming staghorn calculi.

questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with flank pain and hematuria of 12 hours' duration; all other findings are normal. What is the best imaging modality to diagnose the case?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is preferred as the initial imaging modality in children to avoid radiation exposure from CT.

questions.text: What causes the pain associated with a stone in the ureter?
options: Urinary extravasation from a ruptured calyceal fornix
Obstruction of urine flow with distention of renal capsule
originalOptions: Urinary extravasation from a ruptured calyceal fornix
Obstruction of urine flow with distention of renal capsule
questions.correctAnswer: C) Obstruction of urine flow with distention of renal capsule
questions.correctAnswerText: Obstruction of urine flow with distention of renal capsule
questions.explanation: Ureteric colic results from acute distention of the collecting system and renal capsule secondary to obstruction, producing the characteristic fluctuating colicky pain.

questions.text: The most significant factor contributing to stone formation in patients with struvite calculi is:
questions.explanation: Struvite (infection) stones form specifically in the setting of recurrent UTIs with urease-producing organisms such as Proteus, which alkalinize the urine.

questions.text: Factors affecting the probability of spontaneous passage of ureteral calculi include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Spontaneous passage is determined mainly by stone size, location, duration of symptoms, and degree of hydronephrosis — not by the chemical composition of the stone.

questions.text: All of the following treatments of an obstructing ureteral calculus in a pregnant woman are acceptable EXCEPT:
options: Placement of a double-J ureteral stent
originalOptions: Placement of a double-J ureteral stent
questions.explanation: ESWL is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy; ureteroscopy and drainage procedures (JJ stent or nephrostomy) are the acceptable options.

questions.text: Which of the following favors spontaneous passage of stones greater than 10 mm?
questions.explanation: Stones larger than 10 mm have a low likelihood of spontaneous passage regardless of location, gender, or hydration status; active intervention is generally required.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication for ESWL?
questions.explanation: Well-controlled diabetes is not a contraindication to ESWL; true contraindications include pregnancy, coagulopathy, distal obstruction, and an arterial aneurysm near the stone.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to ESWL?
questions.explanation: Stone composition such as calcium oxalate is not a contraindication to ESWL, unlike pregnancy, coagulopathy, and uncontrolled hypertension.

questions.text: Distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) is associated with which type of stones?
questions.explanation: dRTA causes an inability to acidify the urine, producing alkaline urine that predisposes to calcium phosphate stone formation along with nephrocalcinosis.

questions.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) are associated with which of the following stones?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide blocks bicarbonate reabsorption, producing alkaline urine that promotes calcium phosphate stone formation.

questions.text: What are the components of an infection (struvite) stone?
questions.explanation: Struvite (triple phosphate) stones are composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate, formed as a result of urease-producing bacterial infection.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an inhibitor of stone crystallization in metastable urine?
questions.explanation: Phosphate is a stone-forming component (part of calcium phosphate and struvite stones), not an inhibitor; citrate, Tamm-Horsfall protein, and magnesium are recognized inhibitors of crystallization.

questions.text: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a 1.5 cm renal stone and also has coagulopathy. What is the best treatment modality?
questions.explanation: ESWL and PCNL are contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders due to hemorrhage risk; ureteroscopy is a safer alternative in this setting.

questions.text: A patient presents with a staghorn uric acid stone. Which of the following is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: Uric acid stones, even staghorn ones, can be dissolved through urinary alkalinization, avoiding the need for surgical intervention.

questions.text: A patient presents with a lower ureteric stone measuring 8 mm. Which of the following is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: For stones under 10 mm in the lower ureter, ureteroscopy is the recommended first-line treatment.

questions.text: Which stone type is linked with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)?
questions.explanation: Fat malabsorption in IBD causes free fatty acids to bind calcium in the gut, leaving more free oxalate to be absorbed. This leads to enteric hyperoxaluria and the subsequent formation of calcium oxalate stones.

questions.text: What is the cause of stones associated with short bowel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Short bowel syndrome causes fat malabsorption leading to enteric hyperoxaluria, the same mechanism seen in inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.text: What is the best management for small ureteric stones associated with infection?
options: Urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy) plus antibiotics
originalOptions: Urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy) plus antibiotics
questions.correctAnswer: A) Urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy) plus antibiotics
questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy) plus antibiotics
questions.explanation: An infected, obstructed urinary system is a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage combined with antibiotics; delaying decompression for medical expulsive therapy alone risks sepsis.

questions.text: The ureter is divided radiologically into:
questions.explanation: Radiologically, the ureter is divided into upper (renal pelvis to upper border of sacrum), middle (over the sacrum), and lower (sacrum to bladder) segments.

questions.text: What is the gold standard imaging for diagnosing urinary stones?
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT has the highest sensitivity and specificity for detecting urinary stones, including radiolucent stones missed by KUB.

questions.text: Resorptive hypercalciuria leading to calcium stones is usually due to:
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes excessive bone resorption, leading to resorptive hypercalciuria and calcium stone formation.

questions.text: Which type of stone is most commonly associated with UTI?
questions.explanation: Struvite (infection) stones form specifically in association with urease-producing bacterial UTIs such as Proteus.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of calcium oxalate stones?
questions.explanation: Hypercalciuria is the most common metabolic abnormality underlying calcium oxalate stone formation.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of staghorn calculi?
questions.explanation: Proteus is the classic urease-producing organism responsible for most infection (struvite) staghorn calculi.

questions.text: What kind of stone grows in an alkaline environment?
questions.explanation: Struvite stones form in alkaline urine created by urease-splitting bacteria, unlike uric acid and cystine stones, which favor acidic urine.

questions.text: Uric acid stone formation is associated with:
questions.explanation: Uric acid is poorly soluble in acidic urine, so persistently low urinary pH is a key determinant of uric acid stone formation.

questions.text: Which one is NOT a high-risk factor for stone formation?
questions.explanation: Hyperlipidemia is not a recognized risk factor for urolithiasis, unlike hypercalcemia, hyperuricosuria, and recurrent UTI.

questions.text: All of the following affect kidney stone formation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Stone composition is a result of stone formation, not a factor that drives it; hydration, urinary pH, and diet are established contributing factors.

questions.text: What is the appropriate advice for a patient with calcium oxalate stones?
questions.explanation: Increasing fluid intake to maintain a high urine output is the single most effective measure to reduce stone recurrence; calcium restriction is not recommended as it can paradoxically increase oxalate absorption.

questions.text: In which of the following cases is medical expulsive therapy (MET) indicated?
options: 4 mm distal ureteral stone with normal findings and controlled pain
originalOptions: 4 mm distal ureteral stone with normal findings and controlled pain
questions.correctAnswer: B) 4 mm distal ureteral stone with normal findings and controlled pain
questions.correctAnswerText: 4 mm distal ureteral stone with normal findings and controlled pain
questions.explanation: MET with alpha-blockers is appropriate for small, distal, uncomplicated stones with a high likelihood of spontaneous passage and well-controlled pain; larger stones, infection, or hydronephrosis warrant more active intervention.

questions.text: A patient has a 4 mm proximal ureteric stone. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Small stones (<5 mm) have a high likelihood of spontaneous passage and are typically managed conservatively with medical expulsive therapy (e.g., alpha-blockers) and analgesia before considering active intervention.

questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presents with flank pain and microscopic hematuria. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging modality in children to avoid unnecessary radiation exposure from CT.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic feature of a KUB (Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder) X-ray?
options: It can detect the majority of stones
It is of marginal value and cost-ineffective compared to its diagnostic benefit
It is a simple, non-invasive imaging technique
It exposes the patient to radiation
originalOptions: It can detect the majority of stones
It is of marginal value and cost-ineffective compared to its diagnostic benefit
It is a simple, non-invasive imaging technique
It exposes the patient to radiation
questions.correctAnswer: B) It is of marginal value and cost-ineffective compared to its diagnostic benefit
questions.correctAnswerText: It is of marginal value and cost-ineffective compared to its diagnostic benefit
questions.explanation: KUB is actually a cheap, useful modality mainly for monitoring known stones or treatment response, so describing it as cost-ineffective is not an accurate characteristic.

questions.text: A patient has mild hydronephrosis and a 3 mm ureteric stone on CT abdomen, and also has a peptic ulcer. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs are contraindicated in patients with peptic ulcer disease, so tramadol is used as an alternative analgesic for renal colic in this setting.

questions.text: A 60-year-old male with asthma has a 5 mm distal ureteric stone with mild hydronephrosis, and his pain improved with analgesia. What is the appropriate treatment?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Give tramadol, tamsulosin, and antibiotics
questions.explanation: NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with asthma due to bronchospasm risk, so tramadol is used for analgesia, combined with tamsulosin for medical expulsive therapy.

questions.text: In which of the following conditions is a full metabolic stone workup NOT routinely indicated?
questions.explanation: A full metabolic stone workup is reserved for high-risk stone formers based on stone type or recurrence, and is not routinely triggered by osteoporosis alone.

questions.text: The best management of a 3 cm renal stone is:
questions.explanation: PCNL is first-line for large renal stones (>2 cm) due to its superior stone clearance rate compared to ESWL or ureteroscopy.

questions.text: A 27-year-old man with a 3-week history of intermittent mild right flank pain has a radiolucent 6x8 mm filling defect in the distal ureter with mild hydroureteronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pH 5.5, numerous urate crystals, and 8–10 RBC/hpf, with a negative urine culture. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: The radiolucent stone, acidic urine, and urate crystals point to a uric acid stone, which can be dissolved by alkalinizing the urine with potassium citrate.

questions.text: Which of the following is a radiolucent urinary stone?
questions.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain KUB films, unlike calcium-containing stones, which are radio-opaque.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute flank pain, and the following image is obtained. Which imaging study is shown? [img: distaluretericcalculus.png]
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT (CT KUB) is the standard cross-sectional imaging modality used to identify a hyperdense focus along the ureter, confirming a ureteric calculus.

questions.text: A CT scan shows a small hyperdense focus along the distal ureter with mild proximal dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: distaluretericcalculus.png]
questions.explanation: A focal hyperdense lesion within the ureter on non-contrast CT is the classic appearance of a ureteric stone, distinguishing it from soft-tissue lesions such as tumors or clots.

questions.text: All of the following are appropriate management options for a distal ureteric stone EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: PCNL is reserved for large renal (staghorn) stones, not distal ureteric stones; MET, ureteroscopy, and ESWL are all appropriate options for distal ureteric calculi.

questions.text: A KUB and renal ultrasound are performed in a patient with left flank pain. Which of the following pairs correctly matches the expected findings? [img: kubandurinaryultrasound.png]
options: Radiopaque left ureteric stone — moderate left hydronephrosis
Radiolucent left ureteric stone — normal right kidney
originalOptions: Radiopaque left ureteric stone — moderate left hydronephrosis
Radiolucent left ureteric stone — normal right kidney
questions.correctAnswer: A) Radiopaque left ureteric stone — moderate left hydronephrosis
questions.correctAnswerText: Radiopaque left ureteric stone — moderate left hydronephrosis
questions.explanation: KUB typically demonstrates radiopaque stones, while ultrasound is useful for detecting the resulting hydronephrosis from obstruction.

questions.text: All of the following are indications for urgent intervention in a patient with an obstructing ureteric stone EXCEPT:
options: Mild pain adequately controlled with oral analgesia
originalOptions: Mild pain adequately controlled with oral analgesia
questions.correctAnswer: D) Mild pain adequately controlled with oral analgesia
questions.correctAnswerText: Mild pain adequately controlled with oral analgesia
questions.explanation: Well-controlled pain does not require urgent intervention, whereas infected obstruction, bilateral obstruction, and solitary kidney obstruction are true urological emergencies requiring urgent drainage.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs both represent radiolucent stones on plain KUB?
questions.explanation: Uric acid and cystine stones are radiolucent (or poorly radiopaque) on plain X-ray, unlike calcium-containing and struvite stones, which are radiopaque.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs represents appropriate treatment options for an upper ureteric stone?
questions.explanation: ESWL and ureteroscopy are both established, minimally invasive options for treating upper ureteric stones, unlike the other pairs which are inappropriate or unrelated procedures.

questions.text: What is the stone size cut-off below which spontaneous passage is most likely?
questions.explanation: Stones ≤5 mm have a high likelihood of spontaneous passage, while stones >10 mm are unlikely to pass without intervention.

questions.text: Regarding the kidney's hemodynamic response to acute unilateral ureteral obstruction (with a normal contralateral kidney), which of the following best describes the sequence of changes over time?
options: Early (1–2 hours): increased renal blood flow via preglomerular vasodilation → Late (24 hours): decreased renal blood flow and GFR via vasoconstriction
Early (1–2 hours): decreased renal blood flow → Late (24 hours): increased GFR
Renal blood flow remains constant throughout the obstruction
GFR increases progressively throughout the obstruction period
originalOptions: Early (1–2 hours): increased renal blood flow via preglomerular vasodilation → Late (24 hours): decreased renal blood flow and GFR via vasoconstriction
Early (1–2 hours): decreased renal blood flow → Late (24 hours): increased GFR
Renal blood flow remains constant throughout the obstruction
GFR increases progressively throughout the obstruction period
questions.correctAnswer: A) Early (1–2 hours): increased renal blood flow via preglomerular vasodilation → Late (24 hours): decreased renal blood flow and GFR via vasoconstriction
questions.correctAnswerText: Early (1–2 hours): increased renal blood flow via preglomerular vasodilation → Late (24 hours): decreased renal blood flow and GFR via vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: Acute obstruction initially causes vasodilation and increased renal blood flow, but by 24 hours vasoconstrictive mediators (e.g., angiotensin II, thromboxane A2) predominate, reducing renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.text: All of the following dietary factors increase the risk of stone formation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: High fluid intake is protective against stone formation by diluting urine and reducing supersaturation, unlike high protein, high salt, and oxalate-rich foods (chocolate and nuts), which all increase stone risk.

questions.text: Which pair of stones characteristically forms in alkaline urine?
questions.explanation: Both calcium phosphate and struvite (infection) stones form in alkaline urine, whereas uric acid and cystine stones favor acidic urine.

questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for a patient with an 8 mm mid-ureteric stone?
questions.explanation: Ureteroscopy is the preferred treatment for mid-ureteric stones under 10 mm, offering high success rates with minimal invasiveness.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized limitation of KUB X-ray in the diagnosis of urinary stones?
options: It cannot detect any calcified stones
originalOptions: It cannot detect any calcified stones
questions.correctAnswer: A) It cannot detect radiolucent stones
questions.explanation: KUB relies on stone radiopacity, so radiolucent stones such as uric acid stones are not visualized, limiting its diagnostic utility compared to CT.

questions.text: Which pair represents recognized adverse effects of ESWL?
questions.explanation: Hematuria and perirenal hematoma are the classic adverse effects of ESWL due to shock-wave-induced tissue trauma, unlike the other listed complications which are associated with different procedures or drugs.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly pairs stone types with their radiographic appearance on KUB?
options: Uric acid — radiolucent; Calcium oxalate — radiopaque
Calcium phosphate — radiolucent; Uric acid — radiopaque
originalOptions: Uric acid — radiolucent; Calcium oxalate — radiopaque
Calcium phosphate — radiolucent; Uric acid — radiopaque
questions.correctAnswer: A) Uric acid — radiolucent; Calcium oxalate — radiopaque
questions.correctAnswerText: Uric acid — radiolucent; Calcium oxalate — radiopaque
questions.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent while calcium oxalate stones are radiopaque on plain KUB, a key distinguishing feature used in stone classification.

questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding staghorn calculi is correct?
options: Composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate and best managed with PCNL
Composed of uric acid and best managed with ESWL
Composed of cystine and best managed with observation
Composed of calcium oxalate and best managed with medical expulsive therapy
originalOptions: Composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate and best managed with PCNL
Composed of uric acid and best managed with ESWL
Composed of cystine and best managed with observation
Composed of calcium oxalate and best managed with medical expulsive therapy
questions.correctAnswer: A) Composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate and best managed with PCNL
questions.correctAnswerText: Composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate and best managed with PCNL
questions.explanation: Staghorn calculi are typically struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones associated with urease-producing infections, and PCNL is the first-line treatment due to its high stone-free rate for large, complex renal stones.

questions.text: Most common histopathology in testicular tumors:
questions.explanation: Seminoma is the most common single histological subtype of testicular germ cell tumors (~65%) and the most common testicular tumor in adults.

questions.text: Cryptorchidism (undescended testis) is primarily associated with which complication?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism impairs spermatogenesis due to an unsuitable developmental environment and hyperthermia, and also increases testicular cancer risk.

questions.text: Which of the following is an established risk factor for testicular cancer?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism is one of the five well-established risk factors for testicular cancer, raising risk up to 40-fold; smoking, DM, and hypertension are not established risk factors.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor for testicular cancer?
questions.explanation: The established risk factors are white race, cryptorchidism, family history, personal history of testicular cancer, and germ cell neoplasia in situ; maternal preeclampsia is not among them.

questions.text: Testicular tumors most commonly metastasize to which lymph node group?
questions.explanation: Testicular lymphatic drainage follows the gonadal vessels directly to the retroperitoneal/para-aortic nodes, not the inguinal nodes, unless the scrotal skin itself is involved.

questions.text: What is the best initial management for a patient diagnosed with testicular cancer?
questions.explanation: Inguinal radical orchidectomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic; trans-scrotal biopsy or orchidectomy is avoided because it risks seeding the scrotal lymphatics.

questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless testicular mass and elevated β-hCG. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Inguinal radical orchidectomy is the gold-standard initial management for suspected testicular cancer, providing tissue diagnosis while avoiding scrotal contamination.

questions.text: What is the most common presentation of testicular cancer?
questions.explanation: The vast majority of testicular cancers present as a painless testicular mass, often found incidentally or by the patient.

questions.text: A painless testicular mass should be considered which of the following until proven otherwise?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Testicular cancer until proven otherwise
questions.explanation: Any painless, firm intratesticular mass must be assumed malignant until excluded by ultrasound and, if needed, orchidectomy.

questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless, hard scrotal mass he recently noticed. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
originalOptions: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation: Scrotal (Doppler) ultrasound is the first-line investigation to characterize a testicular mass before any biopsy or staging imaging is pursued.

questions.text: A 36-year-old man complains of painless testicular swelling and heaviness with a hard testis on examination, no fever, and a remote history of testicular trauma. Ultrasound suggests a mass. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Testicular mass — inguinal radical orchiectomy
questions.explanation: A remote trauma history is a common distractor; a hard, painless mass confirmed on ultrasound is treated as testicular cancer with inguinal radical orchiectomy.

questions.text: What is the most common complication if undescended testis (UDT) is left untreated?
questions.explanation: Untreated cryptorchidism markedly increases the risk of Germ cell (testicular) malignancy in addition to infertility.

questions.text: A male patient presents with a testicular mass and elevated serum AFP and β-hCG. Which of the following tumor types is most consistent with this marker profile?
questions.explanation: Combined elevation of AFP and β-hCG indicates a nonseminomatous component; pure seminoma never elevates AFP, and "pure" yolk sac tumor typically elevates AFP alone, so embryonal carcinoma (or a mixed tumor) best fits both markers being raised.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a common complication of undescended testis?
questions.explanation: The recognized complications of undescended testis are infertility, malignancy, and torsion; UTI is not a characteristic complication.

questions.text: What is the recommended age for surgical orchidopexy in undescended testis?
questions.explanation: If the testis remains undescended, definitive orchidopexy is ideally performed at 6–12 months of age.

questions.text: Which type of testicular tumor characteristically elevates β-hCG only, without elevating AFP?
questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma secretes β-hCG and is notable for early hematogenous spread, but it never elevates AFP.

questions.text: To which lymph node group does testicular cancer characteristically metastasize?
questions.explanation: Testicular lymphatic drainage follows the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (retroperitoneal) nodes, mirroring the embryologic origin of the testis.

questions.text: What is the most common type of testicular cancer?
questions.explanation: Seminoma accounts for the largest proportion of testicular germ cell tumors and is the most common subtype in adults.

questions.text: What is the most appropriate management for a 4-month-old male with a right-sided undescended testis?
questions.explanation: At 4 months, spontaneous descent may still occur; definitive orchidopexy is reserved for testes still undescended at 6–12 months, so continued observation with follow-up is appropriate now.

questions.text: In a patient presenting with a painless scrotal lump, which diagnosis must be excluded first?
questions.explanation: A painless intratesticular lump is considered malignant until proven otherwise.

questions.text: What is the most appropriate investigation for a patient presenting with a painless scrotal lump?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler
questions.explanation: Doppler ultrasound determines whether the lesion is intratesticular versus extratesticular and solid versus cystic; if suspicious, AFP, β-hCG, and LDH are sent, while trans-scrotal biopsy is avoided due to seeding risk.

questions.text: A patient presents with a painless scrotal lump. Should the assessment proceed urgently rather than as routine follow-up?
questions.explanation: Given the risk of malignancy, a painless scrotal lump requires urgent urological assessment through a suspected-cancer pathway rather than routine follow-up.

questions.text: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, nausea, bradycardia, and hypertension near the end of a prolonged resection. Serum sodium is low. This is best explained by:
options: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
originalOptions: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswer: A) Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswerText: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome results from absorption of hypotonic irrigating solution through open venous sinuses during resection, causing hypervolemic hyponatremia with confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and visual disturbances.

questions.text: Which factor is most associated with increased risk of TUR syndrome?
options: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
originalOptions: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Resection time greater than 90 minutes
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome risk increases with resection times exceeding 90 minutes and is more common in older men; bipolar TURP performed under saline (isotonic) irrigation reduces this risk.

questions.text: A patient requires long-term indwelling catheterization. Compared to latex, silicone catheters are preferred because they:
options: Are only available in smaller sizes
originalOptions: Are only available in smaller sizes
questions.explanation: Silicone catheters induce less tissue inflammation than latex, making them preferable for long-term catheterization, despite latex being cheaper and more widely available.

questions.text: A 24 French Foley catheter has an outer diameter of approximately:
questions.explanation: Catheter French size divided by 3 gives the outer diameter in millimeters; 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized indication for urethral catheterization?
options: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
originalOptions: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption
questions.correctAnswer: A) Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
questions.correctAnswerText: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
questions.explanation: Monitoring urine output is a standard, common indication for catheterization. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, pelvic fracture with urethral disruption) is a contraindication until imaging excludes injury.

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to transurethral Foley catheter placement?
options: Need for a clean urine sample
originalOptions: Need for a clean urine sample
questions.explanation: Suspected urethral injury is a contraindication to urethral catheterization; a retrograde urethrogram should be performed first, and a suprapubic catheter used if drainage is needed.

questions.text: Chronic urinary retention is best distinguished from acute retention by which feature?
options: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
originalOptions: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
questions.correctAnswer: B) Painless, palpable, and percussible bladder
questions.explanation: Chronic retention classically presents as a painless, palpable/percussible bladder due to gradual distension, in contrast to the painful presentation of acute retention.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic heart disease presents with fever of 40°C, HR 125, BP 120/65, and suprapubic tenderness consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis with urinary retention. The most appropriate management is:
options: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
originalOptions: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Prostatic massage to obtain culture, then antibiotics
Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate
questions.correctAnswer: D) Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
questions.correctAnswerText: Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
questions.explanation: In acute bacterial prostatitis, urethral catheterization and instrumentation are contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia; urinary retention should be managed with a suprapubic catheter along with IV antibiotics and admission.

questions.text: Which of the following clinical situations requires urgent decompression of the urinary tract?
options: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
originalOptions: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
questions.correctAnswer: C) An obstructed, infected collecting system
questions.explanation: An obstructed and infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urologic emergency requiring urgent decompression via JJ stent or nephrostomy to prevent sepsis and renal destruction.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of long-term double-J (JJ) ureteral stenting?
questions.explanation: Long-standing catheters (not JJ stents specifically) are linked to stone formation and bladder cancer risk with prolonged indwelling urethral catheters; urothelial cancer is not a typical direct complication attributed to JJ stents, whose common complications are infection, hematuria, and irritative/positional flank pain.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medications used for overactive bladder?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, and confusion, due to inhibition of parasympathetic (muscarinic) activity on the gut and other organs.

questions.text: A fetus is found to have antenatal hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound. Appropriate postnatal evaluation includes:
options: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
originalOptions: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswer: A) Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.explanation: Postnatal workup of antenatal hydronephrosis is guided by severity, using renal ultrasound as the initial test, followed by VCUG (to assess for reflux) and/or renal scan (to assess function/obstruction) as indicated.

questions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have mild hydronephrosis on ultrasound with no symptoms of infection or stone disease. This is most likely explained by:
options: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
originalOptions: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswerText: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.explanation: Mild hydronephrosis in pregnancy, particularly on the right side, is commonly physiological due to compression of the ureter by the enlarging gravid uterus and does not necessarily indicate pathology.

questions.text: A female patient presents with flank pain and fever. She was treated with antibiotics, but after 3 days she still has fever and fatigue. What is the best next step in management?
options: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
originalOptions: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.correctAnswer: C) CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.correctAnswerText: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation: Persistent fever despite 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics for pyelonephritis mandates a contrast CT to exclude a complication such as perinephric/renal abscess, obstruction, or emphysematous pyelonephritis; simply switching antibiotics or relying on ultrasound alone risks missing these findings.

questions.text: Bacterial prostatitis is usually caused by:
options: Ascending infection with enteric gram-negative bacteria
originalOptions: Ascending infection with enteric gram-negative bacteria
questions.correctAnswer: B) Ascending infection with enteric gram-negative bacteria
questions.correctAnswerText: Ascending infection with enteric gram-negative bacteria
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial prostatitis is most commonly caused by ascending infection with enteric gram-negative organisms, chiefly E. coli, rather than by hematogenous spread or anaerobic organisms.

questions.text: In acute bacterial prostatitis, which of the following should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Transurethral instrumentation should be avoided in acute bacterial prostatitis because it can worsen inflammation and precipitate bacteremia; a suprapubic catheter is used instead if urinary retention develops.

questions.text: All of the following bacteria produce urease (potentially causing infection stones) EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and staphylococci commonly produce urease and are linked to struvite (infection) stones, whereas E. coli only rarely secretes urease.

questions.text: Nosocomial urinary tract infections (UTIs):
options: Are only caused by bowel bacteria
Occur in patients who are hospitalized or institutionalized
Can be suppressed by low-dose antimicrobial therapy
originalOptions: Are only caused by bowel bacteria
Occur in patients who are hospitalized or institutionalized
Can be suppressed by low-dose antimicrobial therapy
questions.correctAnswer: C) Occur in patients who are hospitalized or institutionalized
questions.correctAnswerText: Occur in patients who are hospitalized or institutionalized
questions.explanation: Nosocomial UTIs are, by definition, acquired during hospitalization or institutionalization, most often catheter-associated and caused by resistant organisms.

questions.text: Most common organism associated with uncomplicated cystitis:
questions.explanation: E. coli accounts for roughly 80–85% of uncomplicated community-acquired cystitis cases.

questions.text: A 70-year-old female is found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly, non-pregnant women should not be treated, since antibiotics do not improve outcomes and only promote resistance.

questions.text: The virulence factor most important for bacterial adherence in the kidney (pyelonephritis-associated) uropathogenic E. coli is:
questions.explanation: P-Pili (type P fimbriae) bind uroepithelial receptors and confer renal tropism, making them the key adherence factor in pyelonephritis-associated E. coli, distinct from type 1 fimbriae, which mediate bladder mucosal adherence.

questions.text: Which of the following is the virulence factor of uropathogenic E. coli that aids in bladder colonization?
questions.explanation: Pili-1 (type 1 fimbriae) are mannose-sensitive and mediate adherence to bladder mucosa, promoting lower urinary tract colonization, while type P fimbriae mediate upper tract (renal) tropism.

questions.text: Acute pyelonephritis is the most likely diagnosis in a patient presenting with:
options: Focal scar in the renal cortex
originalOptions: Focal scar in the renal cortex
questions.correctAnswer: D) Chills, fever, and flank pain
questions.explanation: Chills, fever, and flank pain with costovertebral angle tenderness form the classic clinical triad of acute pyelonephritis.

questions.text: The most reliable (least contaminated) urine specimen is obtained by:
questions.explanation: Suprapubic aspiration bypasses the urethra entirely and is considered the gold-standard, least-contaminated method of urine collection, though it is rarely used due to its invasiveness.

questions.text: The most sensitive imaging modality for diagnosing a renal abscess is:
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the most sensitive imaging study for renal/perinephric abscess, classically showing a rim-enhancing ("ring sign") lesion.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT classified as a complicated UTI?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Healthy non-pregnant female with UTI
questions.explanation: A UTI in a healthy, non-pregnant, structurally and functionally normal female is uncomplicated; UTIs in males, diabetics, or catheterized patients are complicated due to underlying anatomical or functional abnormalities.

questions.text: Indications for imaging in UTI include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Single episode of uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy female
originalOptions: Single episode of uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy female
questions.correctAnswer: C) Single episode of uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy female
questions.correctAnswerText: Single episode of uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy female
questions.explanation: A single episode of uncomplicated cystitis in an otherwise healthy female does not require imaging and should be treated empirically; imaging is reserved for recurrent, refractory, or complicated presentations.

questions.text: Which of the following is a common cause of recurrent UTIs in premenopausal women?
questions.explanation: Sexual intercourse is a major precipitant of recurrent UTI in premenopausal women; low estrogen becomes the more relevant risk factor after menopause.

questions.text: Colonization of the urinary tract includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Asymptomatic presence in the urinary tract
originalOptions: Asymptomatic presence in the urinary tract
questions.explanation: Colonization refers to bacterial presence, adherence, and multiplication without tissue invasion; invasion of the urothelium with an inflammatory response defines true infection, not colonization.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a bacterial virulence factor in UTIs?
questions.explanation: Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) is a host-derived defense factor that binds bacterial pili and prevents their adherence to the urothelium; it is not a bacterial virulence factor.

questions.text: Sterile pyuria may be seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sterile pyuria means WBCs in the urine with a negative standard culture; an untreated, ordinary bacterial UTI produces pyuria with a positive culture, whereas TB, interstitial nephritis, and stones can cause pyuria with a negative routine culture.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about urinary tract infections?
options: Recurrent UTIs are unrelated to previous episodes
Recurrent UTI risk increases with prior UTI frequency
originalOptions: Recurrent UTIs are unrelated to previous episodes
Recurrent UTI risk increases with prior UTI frequency
questions.correctAnswer: D) Recurrent UTI risk increases with prior UTI frequency
questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent UTI risk increases with prior UTI frequency
questions.explanation: The probability of recurrence increases with the number of previous UTIs and is inversely related to the time between episodes, making prior infection frequency the strongest predictor of recurrence.

questions.text: A pregnant woman in her first trimester with G6PD deficiency presents with bacterial cystitis. What is the appropriate antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Cephalexin is safe in both pregnancy and G6PD deficiency; nitrofurantoin should be avoided in G6PD deficiency, trimethoprim (TMP) is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonist), and fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with pelvic pain and fever; a contrast-enhanced CT was performed. What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: acutepyelonephritis.png]
questions.explanation: The combination of fever with pelvic/flank pain and a CT perfusion-defect appearance is characteristic of acute pyelonephritis rather than simple obstruction, abscess, or gas-forming infection.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of community-acquired UTI?
questions.explanation: E. coli is responsible for approximately 85% of community-acquired UTIs.

questions.text: Which of the following features differentiates pyelonephritis from cystitis?
questions.explanation: Costovertebral angle (renal angle) tenderness reflects renal parenchymal/pelvic involvement and is specific to pyelonephritis, whereas frequency, dysuria, and pyuria can occur in both cystitis and pyelonephritis.

questions.text: Fever, chills, and flank pain are most likely to indicate:
questions.explanation: Fever, chills, and flank pain form the classic presentation of acute pyelonephritis, distinguishing it from lower tract infections such as cystitis or urethritis, which are typically afebrile.

questions.text: A male with acute bacterial prostatitis was started on IV antibiotics but showed no improvement after 72 hours. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Failure to improve after appropriate IV antibiotics should prompt TRUS to evaluate for a prostatic abscess requiring drainage; prostatic massage is contraindicated because of bacteremia risk.

questions.text: A case of pyelonephritis with persistent symptoms after 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Lack of clinical response after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy in pyelonephritis warrants a contrast CT to look for an abscess, obstruction, or other complication.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a host defense mechanism against urinary tract infections?
questions.explanation: Type 1 pili are a bacterial virulence factor that promotes adherence, not a host defense mechanism; urine flow, urothelial exfoliation, and the immune response all protect the host.

questions.text: In which of the following cases should asymptomatic bacteriuria be treated?
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because of the risk of progression to pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes; it is not routinely treated in diabetics, patients with neurogenic bladder, or the elderly.

questions.text: Which of the following is classified as a complicated UTI?
options: Isolated infection with no risk factors
originalOptions: Isolated infection with no risk factors
questions.explanation: A UTI in a patient with an indwelling catheter is classified as complicated due to the anatomical/functional abnormality predisposing to infection and reducing treatment efficacy.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with increased UTI-related morbidity?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy increases UTI-related morbidity because untreated infection can progress to pyelonephritis with adverse maternal and fetal outcomes.

questions.text: The presence of air (gas) in the urine is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Pneumaturia is gas in the urine, caused by recent catheterization, an enteric fistula, or infection with a gas-forming organism.

questions.text: What is the best urine sample for the diagnosis of urethritis?
questions.explanation: First-void urine concentrates urethral secretions and organisms and is the preferred specimen for diagnosing urethritis, unlike midstream or suprapubic samples, which are used for bladder or upper tract infections.

questions.text: In which condition is bacteriuria most dangerous?
questions.explanation: Bacteriuria in pregnancy carries the highest risk because of its potential to progress to pyelonephritis and cause pregnancy complications, which is why it is screened for and treated even when asymptomatic.

questions.text: Which of the following medications is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: Sulfonamide-containing agents such as cotrimoxazole can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients and should be avoided.

questions.text: The presence of nitrites in urine indicates infection with:
questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria (e.g., E. coli) reduce urinary nitrate to nitrite, which is detected on dipstick testing; gram-positive organisms and fungi typically do not produce this reaction.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute bacterial prostatitis. What is the appropriate management?
options: Prostatic massage followed by sample collection
Discharge on oral antibiotics without workup
Obtain a urine culture and start appropriate antibiotics
originalOptions: Prostatic massage followed by sample collection
Discharge on oral antibiotics without workup
Obtain a urine culture and start appropriate antibiotics
questions.correctAnswer: D) Obtain a urine culture and start appropriate antibiotics
questions.correctAnswerText: Obtain a urine culture and start appropriate antibiotics
questions.explanation: Management of acute bacterial prostatitis is based on obtaining a urine culture and promptly starting antibiotics (IV if systemically ill); prostatic massage is avoided because of bacteremia risk, and catheterization is reserved for urinary retention rather than performed routinely.

questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with irritative voiding symptoms, fever, and tachycardia. Digital rectal examination could not be tolerated due to pain. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transurethral catheter to obtain a urine sample
Suprapubic catheter to obtain a urine sample
Obtain a midstream urine sample and start empirical antibiotics
originalOptions: Transurethral catheter to obtain a urine sample
Suprapubic catheter to obtain a urine sample
Obtain a midstream urine sample and start empirical antibiotics
questions.correctAnswer: D) Obtain a midstream urine sample and start empirical antibiotics
questions.correctAnswerText: Obtain a midstream urine sample and start empirical antibiotics
questions.explanation: In suspected acute bacterial prostatitis, a midstream urine sample should be collected and empirical antibiotics started promptly; transurethral instrumentation is avoided due to bacteremia risk, and suprapubic catheterization is reserved for urinary retention, not routine sampling.

questions.text: Bacterial urinary tract infections typically involve:
questions.explanation: Most UTIs are caused by a single uropathogenic strain (most often E. coli) ascending from the bowel flora, rather than being polymicrobial or hematogenous in origin.

questions.text: A patient with persistent left flank pain is diagnosed with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. What is the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic destructive renal infection that typically destroys the affected kidney's function; nephrectomy is the definitive treatment.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of pneumaturia?
questions.explanation: Pneumaturia results from recent catheterization, an enteric fistula (as with diverticulitis, IBD, or colon cancer), or infection with gas-forming organisms; an ectopic ureter is unrelated to gas in the urine.

questions.text: Which of the following typically presents as a UTI without fever?
questions.explanation: Cystitis (lower UTI) typically presents with frequency, dysuria, and urgency without fever, whereas pyelonephritis, prostatitis, and renal abscess are usually associated with systemic fever.

questions.text: What is the key difference between prostatitis and cystitis?
questions.explanation: Acute prostatitis is a parenchymal infection causing systemic symptoms (fever, perineal pain, a tender gland on DRE), while cystitis is a mucosal bladder infection causing irritative voiding symptoms that is rarely associated with fever.

questions.text: Which organism is the classic cause of urease-associated infection (struvite) stones?
questions.explanation: Proteus is the classic and most common urease-producing organism responsible for struvite (infection) stones, though Klebsiella can produce urease to a lesser extent.

questions.text: Dysuria occurring at the very beginning of urination suggests involvement of the:
questions.explanation: Initial (beginning-of-stream) symptoms localize to the urethra, consistent with urethritis, as opposed to total or terminal symptoms, which point to bladder or prostatic urethral origin.

questions.text: A febrile diabetic patient presents with flank pain. Which imaging study is most appropriate to evaluate this presentation?
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is the imaging modality of choice to fully characterize renal infection in a febrile, immunocompromised (diabetic) patient with flank pain, as ultrasound alone cannot reliably detect renal inflammation.

questions.text: A febrile diabetic patient presents with flank pain and undergoes contrast-enhanced CT, shown below. Which of the following best describes the expected findings? [img: dmpyelonephritis.png]
options: Wedge-shaped perfusion defect with an enlarged kidney
Calyceal dilatation with a large staghorn calculus
originalOptions: Wedge-shaped perfusion defect with an enlarged kidney
Calyceal dilatation with a large staghorn calculus
questions.correctAnswer: B) Wedge-shaped perfusion defect with an enlarged kidney
questions.correctAnswerText: Wedge-shaped perfusion defect with an enlarged kidney
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial infection causes constriction of peripheral arterioles, producing wedge-shaped perfusion defects and renal enlargement on contrast CT; gas within the parenchyma would instead suggest emphysematous pyelonephritis.

questions.text: A febrile diabetic patient presents with flank pain. Contrast-enhanced CT, shown below, reveals a wedge-shaped perfusion defect with an enlarged kidney. What is the most probable diagnosis? [img: dmpyelonephritis.png]
questions.explanation: Fever, flank pain, and a wedge-shaped perfusion defect on CT are classic for acute pyelonephritis; the absence of gas argues against emphysematous pyelonephritis, and there is no described rim-enhancing collection to suggest abscess.

questions.text: A diabetic patient is diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis based on the clinical picture and CT findings shown below. What is the primary indication for hospital admission in this patient? [img: dmpyelonephritis.png]
options: Immunocompromised state secondary to diabetes mellitus
originalOptions: Immunocompromised state secondary to diabetes mellitus
questions.correctAnswer: C) Immunocompromised state secondary to diabetes mellitus
questions.correctAnswerText: Immunocompromised state secondary to diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus renders the patient immunocompromised and at higher risk of complicated pyelonephritis (including emphysematous pyelonephritis), which is an indication for admission and closer monitoring.

questions.text: A patient with chronic flank pain undergoes CT of the kidney, shown below. Which of the following best describes the CT findings? [img: xanthogranulomatous.png]
options: Enlarged left kidney with a hyperdense renal pelvic stone and destroyed parenchyma
originalOptions: Enlarged left kidney with a hyperdense renal pelvic stone and destroyed parenchyma
questions.correctAnswer: B) Enlarged left kidney with a hyperdense renal pelvic stone and destroyed parenchyma
questions.correctAnswerText: Enlarged left kidney with a hyperdense renal pelvic stone and destroyed parenchyma
questions.explanation: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis classically shows an enlarged, hydronephrotic kidney with a large renal pelvic calculus and destruction of the parenchyma by lipid-laden macrophages, often mimicking RCC radiologically.

questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis based on the CT findings shown below. Which of the following combinations of features is most consistent with this diagnosis? [img: xanthogranulomatous.png]
options: Painless gross hematuria with weight loss
Sudden severe colicky pain with hematuria only
Chronic flank pain, weight loss, and malaise
originalOptions: Painless gross hematuria with weight loss
Sudden severe colicky pain with hematuria only
Chronic flank pain, weight loss, and malaise
questions.correctAnswer: C) Chronic flank pain, weight loss, and malaise
questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic flank pain, weight loss, and malaise
questions.explanation: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic, destructive infection presenting with chronic flank pain, fever, malaise, and weight loss, distinct from the acute colicky pain of stone disease or the scrotal pain of testicular pathology.

questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis based on the CT findings shown below. Which pair of organisms is most commonly implicated as causative? [img: xanthogranulomatous.png]
questions.explanation: Proteus is reported as the most common causative organism in xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, with E. coli also commonly implicated.

questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis based on the CT findings shown below. What is the definitive treatment? [img: xanthogranulomatous.png]
questions.explanation: Because the affected kidney is almost always hydronephrotic, obstructed, and functionally destroyed, nephrectomy is the standard definitive treatment for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

questions.text: A newly married woman presents with irritative urinary symptoms consistent with "honeymoon cystitis." Which of the following correctly pairs the most likely causative organism with the typical antibiotic treatment duration?
questions.explanation: "Honeymoon cystitis" is uncomplicated cystitis related to intercourse, most commonly caused by E. coli and treated with a short course of oral antibiotics (typically 3–5 days depending on the agent chosen); routine culture is not required in a typical uncomplicated case.

questions.text: Which pair of organisms below are BOTH urease-producing organisms that can cause urinary tract infection?
questions.explanation: Proteus and Klebsiella are both urease-producing organisms capable of alkalinizing urine and promoting struvite (infection) stone formation, unlike E. coli, which rarely secretes urease.

questions.text: Which pair of organisms is most typically implicated in obstructive (stone-associated) pyelonephritis?
questions.explanation: E. coli and stone-forming/urease-producing organisms such as Proteus are typically implicated in obstructive pyelonephritis associated with infected calculi.

questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates obstructive from non-obstructive acute pyelonephritis?
options: Both are managed identically with oral antibiotics alone
Obstructive pyelonephritis has an underlying blockage causing impaired drainage and risk of rapid deterioration/urosepsis, while non-obstructive pyelonephritis has normal urinary drainage
originalOptions: Both are managed identically with oral antibiotics alone
Obstructive pyelonephritis has an underlying blockage causing impaired drainage and risk of rapid deterioration/urosepsis, while non-obstructive pyelonephritis has normal urinary drainage
questions.correctAnswer: D) Obstructive pyelonephritis has an underlying blockage causing impaired drainage and risk of rapid deterioration/urosepsis, while non-obstructive pyelonephritis has normal urinary drainage
questions.correctAnswerText: Obstructive pyelonephritis has an underlying blockage causing impaired drainage and risk of rapid deterioration/urosepsis, while non-obstructive pyelonephritis has normal urinary drainage
questions.explanation: An obstructed, infected kidney is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression (JJ stent or nephrostomy) because of the risk of rapid deterioration and urosepsis, unlike non-obstructive pyelonephritis, which is managed with antibiotics alone.

questions.text: Which pair correctly represents the two main routes of bacterial entry into the urinary tract?
options: Hematogenous and direct extension from bowel perforation only
originalOptions: Hematogenous and direct extension from bowel perforation only
questions.explanation: Most UTIs occur via the ascending route (bacteria from the bowel reservoir ascending through the urethra), while hematogenous spread is an uncommon route seen mainly in immunocompromised patients and neonates.

questions.text: Regarding recurrent urinary tract infection, which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Persistent infection always involves reintroduction of bacteria from outside the urinary tract
Reinfection indicates an infected stone or prostate as the source
Reinfection involves a new organism introduced from outside the urinary tract
Reinfection and persistent infection are managed identically regardless of cause
originalOptions: Persistent infection always involves reintroduction of bacteria from outside the urinary tract
Reinfection indicates an infected stone or prostate as the source
Reinfection involves a new organism introduced from outside the urinary tract
Reinfection and persistent infection are managed identically regardless of cause
questions.correctAnswer: C) Reinfection involves a new organism introduced from outside the urinary tract
questions.correctAnswerText: Reinfection involves a new organism introduced from outside the urinary tract
